title: Towards standardisation of average grain size measurement of additively manufactured microstructures using EBSD
comment: 24 pages, 8 figures, presented at the European Microbeam Analysis Society (EMAS) meeting: 18th European Workshop on Modern Developments and Applications in Microbeam Analysis, 11-15 May 2025, TecnoCampus, Mataró (Barcelona), Spain
summary:
Additively manufactured (AM) alloys have heterogeneous microstructures with broad grain size distributions and highly anisotropic and/or non-convex grain shapes. AM components can have complex geometries and porosity which may affect the local microstructure. Currently there is no electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD)-based grain size measurement standard suitable for typical AM materials.
  An interlaboratory comparison study was conducted to find out what grain size metrics and summary statistics are currently used to describe average grain size. Participants were asked to measure and report the average grain size from the same EBSD map dataset. Detailed reports have been published in Reference [1]. Based on these results, we have tested and propose recommendations for a new standard for measuring average grain size in AM materials. The present work demonstrates the suitability and limitations of the proposal across several different Ni and Al AM components.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the lack of an EBSD-based grain size measurement standard for additively manufactured (AM) alloys, which have heterogeneous microstructures. An interlaboratory study revealed current practices, and based on findings, a new standard for measuring average grain size in AM materials is proposed and tested on Ni and Al AM components.
AI.motivation: AM alloys exhibit heterogeneous microstructures (broad grain size distributions, anisotropic/non-convex grain shapes) and complex geometries/porosity that affect local microstructure, yet no EBSD-based grain size measurement standard exists for these materials.
AI.method: An interlaboratory comparison study was conducted where participants measured average grain size from the same EBSD map dataset. Based on the results, recommendations for a new grain size measurement standard were developed and tested on multiple Ni and Al AM components.
AI.result: The study identified current grain size metrics and summary statistics used by the community, leading to a proposed standard whose suitability and limitations were evaluated across different AM materials (Ni and Al alloys).
AI.conclusion: A new EBSD-based grain size measurement standard for AM materials is proposed, with demonstrated applicability to Ni and Al AM components, though limitations exist that warrant further consideration.

title: Comparing Spatially Periodic Feedback and Space-Time Modulation for Unidirectional Wave Propagation in a 1D Mass-Spring-Damper System
summary: Unidirectional wave propagation has emerged as a key concept in the dynamics of non-reciprocal mechanical and acoustic metamaterials. This work investigates two fundamentally distinct strategies for achieving directional wave propagation in a periodic one-dimensional mass-spring-damper lumped system: space-time modulation and spatially periodic feedback. In the first approach, the stiffness is modulated periodically in both space and time. The resulting space-time periodic system is analyzed using a Plane Wave Expansion (PWE) formulation based on the Bloch-Floquet theory to obtain the dispersion relation. The traveling modulation produces asymmetric dispersion diagrams and directional band gaps, within which elastic waves propagate preferentially in a single direction due to broken time-reversal symmetry. In the second approach, non-reciprocity is introduced through a spatially periodic feedback action. The force can depend on the displacement and/or its derivatives, such as velocity or acceleration, and is applied to the masses along the system. The lumped system with a finite number of unit cells is modeled using classical mechanics principles, yielding a state-space model of the system. The active mechanism can generate directional amplification or attenuation via the non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE), characterized by boundary-localized modes identified by a topological invariant, the winding number. The stability of the space-time periodic system is assessed through the Lyapunov-Floquet theory. In the periodic feedback case, stability is investigated using the eigenvalues of the state matrix. These results provide design guidelines for directional wave propagation in elastic waveguides.

AI.tldr: This paper compares two strategies for achieving directional wave propagation in a 1D mass-spring-damper system: (1) space-time modulation of stiffness, which breaks time-reversal symmetry and creates directional band gaps, and (2) spatially periodic feedback control, which induces non-reciprocity via the non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE) and enables directional amplification/attenuation. Stability is assessed via Lyapunov-Floquet theory (modulation) and eigenvalue analysis (feedback).
AI.motivation: To investigate and contrast two fundamentally distinct approaches—space-time modulation and spatially periodic feedback—for achieving unidirectional wave propagation in mechanical/acoustic metamaterials, providing design guidelines for non-reciprocal waveguides.
AI.method: A one-dimensional periodic mass-spring-damper lumped system is analyzed. The first approach uses space-time periodic stiffness modulation, analyzed via Plane Wave Expansion (PWE) based on Bloch-Floquet theory. The second approach introduces spatially periodic feedback with force depending on displacement/velocity/acceleration, modeled via state-space formulation. Stability is evaluated using Lyapunov-Floquet theory (modulation) and eigenvalue analysis (feedback).
AI.result: Space-time modulation yields asymmetric dispersion diagrams and directional band gaps enabling preferential wave propagation. Spatially periodic feedback generates directional amplification/attenuation through the non-Hermitian skin effect, characterized by boundary-localized modes and a topological winding number invariant.
AI.conclusion: Both strategies offer distinct mechanisms for directional wave propagation—time-reversal symmetry breaking via modulation and non-Hermitian topology via feedback—and the stability analyses provide practical design guidelines for non-reciprocal elastic waveguides.

title: Decoupling heat and electricity: A thermal invisible gateway
summary: The Wiedemann-Franz law couples electrical and thermal conductivity, making high electrical conduction with low thermal conduction a major challenge. To overcome this, we designed an active thermal metasurface (ATMS) - based thermal invisible gateway that decouples thermal and electrical paths. Built on a copper substrate with a dumbbell-shaped bridge, the structure suppresses heat flow via directional compensation while allowing unimpeded electrical conduction. Room-temperature experiments show an effective thermal conductivity below 10^-3 W m^-1 K^-1 (near zero, air-like insulation) and an electrical conductivity up to 2.8x10^7 S m^-1 (metal-level). Unlike conventional material-modification approaches, our work uses macroscopic structural design to break the intrinsic coupling, offering a promising solution for applications like on-chip interconnects and wearable electronics.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an active thermal metasurface (ATMS) with a dumbbell-shaped bridge on a copper substrate that decouples thermal and electrical conductivity, achieving near-zero thermal conductivity (~10^-3 W m^-1 K^-1) while maintaining metal-level electrical conductivity (2.8x10^7 S m^-1), breaking the Wiedemann-Franz law through macroscopic structural design.
AI.motivation: The Wiedemann-Franz law inherently couples electrical and thermal conductivity, making it extremely challenging to achieve high electrical conduction simultaneously with low thermal conduction, which is needed for applications like on-chip interconnects and wearable electronics.
AI.method: An active thermal metasurface (ATMS) was designed using a copper substrate with a dumbbell-shaped bridge structure that directionally compensates and suppresses heat flow while allowing unimpeded electrical conduction.
AI.result: Room-temperature experiments demonstrated an effective thermal conductivity below 10^-3 W m^-1 K^-1 (near zero, air-like insulation) and an electrical conductivity up to 2.8x10^7 S m^-1 (metal-level).
AI.conclusion: Unlike conventional material-modification approaches, this work uses macroscopic structural design to break the intrinsic coupling of the Wiedemann-Franz law, offering a promising solution for applications such as on-chip interconnects and wearable electronics.

title: Reconfigurable Multistate MRAM Synapses with Vortex STNO based Neurons for Scalable In-Memory Convolutional Neural Networks
summary: Magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ)-based magnetic random-access memory (MRAM) is a promising platform for neuromorphic and in-memory computing owing to its non-volatility, high endurance, fast switching dynamics and CMOS compatibility. However, conventional spin-transfer torque and spin-orbit torque MRAM implementations for neural networks often suffer from high critical switching currents, large latency, thermal instability and significant read-write overheads. Here, we demonstrate a unified multistate MRAM-spin-torque nano-oscillator (STNO) architecture that integrates synapses and neurons on a single chip for convolutional neural network (CNN) applications. The system employs 1x8 multistate MRAM arrays as programmable synapses coupled with a vortex-based STNO neuron, enabling both individual and collective programming through fieldline-driven write channels. Multiple configurable resistance states are achieved by tuning internal and external magnetic fields together with bias currents, allowing quantized positive and negative synaptic weights for configurable kernel and pooling operations. The proposed architecture is evaluated through simulation on MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10, Google Speech Commands (GSC) and RadioML datasets, achieving accuracy of 99.76%, 87.93%, 78.14%, 87.96% and 56.46% respectively. Based on fabricated device dimensions, the complete architecture occupies ~6171.2 μm2 with an average energy consumption of 200.08 pJ per training and inference cycle for MNIST, highlighting its potential for scalable low-power neuromorphic computing

AI.tldr: This paper presents a unified multistate MRAM-STNO architecture that integrates both synapses and neurons on a single chip for CNN applications, achieving competitive accuracy across multiple datasets (MNIST 99.76%, SVHN 87.93%, CIFAR-10 78.14%, GSC 87.96%, RadioML 56.46%) with a compact footprint (~6171.2 μm²) and low energy consumption (200.08 pJ/cycle for MNIST).
AI.motivation: Conventional STT-MRAM and SOT-MRAM implementations for neural networks suffer from high critical switching currents, large latency, thermal instability, and significant read-write overheads. There is a need for a more efficient MTJ-based architecture that overcomes these limitations for neuromorphic and in-memory computing.
AI.method: The authors propose a unified multistate MRAM-STNO architecture using 1x8 multistate MRAM arrays as programmable synapses coupled with a vortex-based STNO neuron. Multiple configurable resistance states are achieved by tuning internal and external magnetic fields with bias currents. Fieldline-driven write channels enable individual and collective programming, supporting quantized positive and negative synaptic weights for kernel and pooling operations in CNNs.
AI.result: The architecture achieved 99.76% accuracy on MNIST, 87.93% on SVHN, 78.14% on CIFAR-10, 87.96% on Google Speech Commands, and 56.46% on RadioML. The complete design occupies ~6171.2 μm² with average energy consumption of 200.08 pJ per training/inference cycle for MNIST.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multistate MRAM-STNO architecture demonstrates potential for scalable, low-power neuromorphic computing by successfully integrating synapses and neurons on-chip with competitive accuracy and efficient resource utilization across multiple benchmark datasets.

title: Multifractal Complexity of the Chandler Wobble and Its Anomalous Disappearance (2015--2020): A MFDFA Study
summary: The Chandler wobble (CW) -- the $\sim$433-day free nutation of Earth's rotation pole -- experienced an anomalous near-disappearance between 2015 and 2020, followed by a re-excitation with an approximately $180^{\circ}$ phase reversal. Using Multifractal Detrended Fluctuation Analysis (MFDFA) applied to more than six decades (1962--2024) of daily IERS EOP C04 polar motion data, this study provides the first multifractal characterisation of the CW and its recent anomaly. Global MFDFA shows that the residual polar motion components and the CW amplitude are genuine multifractal processes with strongly $q$-dependent generalised Hurst exponents and broad singularity spectra. Surrogate-data tests with shuffled and phase-randomised ensembles demonstrate that this multifractality originates from the combined action of long-range temporal correlations and heavy-tailed excitation statistics. A sliding-window analysis reveals a pronounced collapse in long-range persistence and multifractal spectral width of the geometric polar motion signal several years before and during the 2015--2020 amplitude minimum, indicating a genuine dynamical regime change rather than a simple suppression of oscillation amplitude. In contrast, the amplitude- and phase-related variables retain broad multifractal spectra and stable scaling exponents across all epochs, revealing a dynamical decoupling between the geometry of the CW and the multiscale structure of its amplitude and phase fluctuations. These findings highlight the CW amplitude as an exceptionally multifractal integrator of geophysical excitation and suggest that multifractal metrics may provide early-warning indicators of major transitions in Earth rotation dynamics.

AI.tldr: This study provides the first multifractal characterization of the Chandler wobble using MFDFA on 62 years of polar motion data, revealing that the 2015–2020 amplitude minimum coincided with a collapse in long-range persistence and multifractal spectral width—indicating a dynamical regime change, not just amplitude suppression—and demonstrating a decoupling between geometric signal structure and amplitude/phase fluctuations.
AI.motivation: The Chandler wobble experienced an anomalous near-disappearance between 2015 and 2020 with a phase reversal; the motivation is to characterize this anomaly from a multifractal perspective to understand the underlying dynamics and potential early-warning indicators.
AI.method: Multifractal Detrended Fluctuation Analysis (MFDFA) applied to daily IERS EOP C04 polar motion data from 1962 to 2024, including global MFDFA, surrogate-data tests (shuffled and phase-randomized), and sliding-window analysis to track temporal evolution of multifractal metrics.
AI.result: Residual polar motion and CW amplitude are genuine multifractal processes; multifractality arises from long-range correlations and heavy-tailed excitation statistics; sliding-window analysis reveals a collapse in long-range persistence and spectral width before/during the 2015–2020 minimum; amplitude and phase variables retain broad spectra and stable exponents, showing dynamical decoupling.
AI.conclusion: The CW amplitude is an exceptionally multifractal integrator of geophysical excitation; multifractal metrics may serve as early-warning indicators of major transitions in Earth rotation dynamics.

title: WF-Bench: A Benchmark for Neural Network WaveFunction Expressivity and Scaling Laws
summary: We present a comprehensive benchmarking dataset and empirical scaling law analysis for neural network wavefunctions by matching them to a wide spectrum of famous many body target wavefunctions. The dataset, WF-Bench, spans multiple distinct regimes of strongly correlated quantum matter, including topological states, Wigner crystals, and superconducting wavefunctions, providing a diverse and challenging test bed for neural network wavefunction expressivity. We introduce a systematic and reproducible benchmarking protocol for target wavefunction matching, enabling consistent performance evaluation across different neural network wavefunction architectures. By using wavefunction fidelity as the uniform metric, we discover empirical scaling laws that characterize how representability depends on system size and key model parameters, including number of determinant and model depth. By applying our benchmark protocol on Psiformer and Ferminet, we show that WF-Bench establishes a unified dataset driven framework for evaluating and comparing neural network wavefunctions and for guiding the design of future architectures.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces WF-Bench, a comprehensive benchmarking dataset for neural network wavefunctions, covering diverse many-body quantum states (topological, Wigner crystals, superconducting). It proposes a systematic protocol using wavefunction fidelity as the metric, discovers empirical scaling laws relating representability to system size and model parameters, and benchmarks Psiformer and Ferminet architectures.
AI.motivation: To address the lack of standardized, diverse benchmarks for evaluating neural network wavefunction expressivity across different strongly correlated quantum regimes, enabling fair comparison and guiding architecture design.
AI.method: Constructing WF-Bench dataset with diverse target wavefunctions (topological, Wigner crystal, superconducting); using wavefunction fidelity as a uniform metric; performing systematic scaling law analysis relating system size, number of determinants, and model depth to representability; applying the protocol to Psiformer and Ferminet.
AI.result: Empirical scaling laws were discovered characterizing how representability depends on system size, number of determinants, and model depth. Psiformer and Ferminet were successfully benchmarked, demonstrating WF-Bench's utility for comparing neural network wavefunction architectures.
AI.conclusion: WF-Bench provides a unified, dataset-driven framework for evaluating and comparing neural network wavefunctions, enabling reproducible benchmarking and guiding future architecture design.

title: Graph-based emulation of $d$-dimensional curved spaces with superconducting arrays
summary: We introduce a framework for emulating graphs and, through them, curved spaces of arbitrary dimension, using arrays of superconducting wires. The array consists of two stacked layers of wires, horizontal and vertical, such that wires are parallel within each layer and perpendicular between layers. By discretizing a space into a graph, assigning a superconducting wire with a rigid phase to each vertex, and coupling pairs of wires through Josephson junctions along the graph edges, arbitrary geometries and topologies can be engineered in a controlled setting. The superconducting phases then realize scalar field theories on the emergent geometry. We establish experimentally realistic conditions for implementing these architectures and develop a dictionary relating measurable circuit observables to quantities in the emulated field theory. As an application, we develop the implementation of hyperbolic (Anti-de Sitter) spaces of constant negative curvature and use them as an experimentally accessible platform to explore holographic duality in arbitrary dimensions. We investigate the effects of disorder in the Josephson couplings, which translate into metric variations in the bulk-boundary correspondence, and analyze their impact on boundary scaling exponents both analytically and numerically, finding that holographic duality remains robust even in the presence of strong disorder. Beyond holography, the framework opens a broad range of architectural possibilities, including the exploration of physics on highly nontrivial graphs and toy models of dynamical spacetimes.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a framework for emulating curved spaces of arbitrary dimension using arrays of superconducting wires coupled via Josephson junctions, enabling experimental exploration of holographic duality and field theories on emergent geometries.
AI.motivation: To create an experimentally accessible platform for emulating curved spaces (especially Anti-de Sitter spaces) and exploring holographic duality, as well as field theories on arbitrary geometries and topologies, in a controlled superconducting circuit setting.
AI.method: The framework uses two stacked layers of superconducting wires (horizontal and vertical, perpendicular between layers). Space is discretized into a graph with each vertex assigned a superconducting wire (rigid phase) and edges connected via Josephson junctions. This emulates scalar field theories on the emergent geometry, with circuit observables mapped to field theory quantities.
AI.result: Established experimentally realistic conditions for implementation. Demonstrated hyperbolic (AdS) space emulation. Analyzed disorder effects in Josephson couplings (metric variations in bulk-boundary correspondence) analytically and numerically, finding holographic duality remains robust under strong disorder.
AI.conclusion: The framework opens broad architectural possibilities beyond holography, including exploration of physics on nontrivial graphs and toy models of dynamical spacetimes.

title: Quantum Light Nano-Imaging
summary: Entanglement and quantum correlations are central to the physics of quantum materials, yet they have remained notoriously difficult to probe experimentally. Probing these phenomena in solids requires quantum optical probes that operate at the native length and time scales of material excitations, below the diffraction limit of light. Developing the requisite tools has previously been infeasible due to the extremely weak intensities of state-of-the-art quantum light sources and extreme inefficiency of near-field light-matter interactions. In this work, we circumvent these challenges and develop a quantum light scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscope (q-SNOM) that can explore the broad domain of solid-state quantum effects at length scales below the diffraction limit. In its first application, we image in real space the self-interference of single hybrid light-matter quasiparticles in a van der Waals semiconductor, providing a direct nanoscale visualization of the wave-particle duality. We also introduce a polaritonic time-of-flight metrology that exploits the temporal correlations among entangled photons to observe the quasiparticle propagation dynamics with femtosecond resolution. This work sets the stage for nanoscale exploration and control of quantum effects in materials.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a quantum light scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscope (q-SNOM) that enables nanoscale probing of quantum phenomena in solids below the diffraction limit. It demonstrates real-space imaging of single hybrid light-matter quasiparticle self-interference and introduces polaritonic time-of-flight metrology using entangled photon correlations for femtosecond-resolution dynamics.
AI.motivation: Quantum correlations in materials are difficult to probe experimentally because they require quantum optical techniques operating below the diffraction limit, which was previously infeasible due to weak quantum light sources and inefficient near-field interactions.
AI.method: The authors developed q-SNOM (quantum scanning near-field optical microscope) that combines quantum light sources with near-field optical microscopy to overcome intensity and efficiency limitations.
AI.result: Real-space imaging of single hybrid light-matter quasiparticle (polariton) self-interference in a van der Waals semiconductor, demonstrating nanoscale wave-particle duality. Also developed polaritonic time-of-flight metrology using entangled photon temporal correlations with femtosecond resolution.
AI.conclusion: This work enables nanoscale exploration and control of quantum effects in materials, opening new avenues for studying solid-state quantum phenomena at their native length and time scales.

title: DFT Accuracy on Crystal Structure Prediction with Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
summary: We present an evaluation of CSP-MACE-Å, a machine learning interatomic potential intended to replace DFT in crystal structure prediction (CSP). We decompose the total energy into separate intramolecular and intermolecular components. For the intramolecular component, we adopt the MACE-POLAR architecture and train it on the OMol25 dataset. The intermolecular component combines three terms: an intermolecular contribution from the MACE-POLAR model, a long-range dispersion term with the functional form of the XDM correction, and a learned delta model trained to reproduce B86bPBE-XDM intermolecular energies. The learned delta model is trained on residual intermolecular targets derived from 50,000 B86bPBE-XDM calculations on molecular crystal structures. On an evaluation set composed of 19 compounds, including a salt, selected from AstraZeneca's previous CSP publications, CSP-MACE-Å achieves performance comparable to PBE DFT with the Neumann-Perrin dispersion correction. On a second evaluation set composed of 28 compounds, including cocrystals and salts, collated from the seven CSP blind tests, CSP-MACE-Å achieves performance close to B86bPBE-XDM DFT. In both evaluation sets, reranking with harmonic free energies substantially improves performance relative to ranking by energy alone. Across our evaluation suite, CSP-MACE-Å is shown to outperform the MACE-POLAR-1 and UMA-OMC foundation models. Lastly, on a set of five compounds, CSP-MACE-Å is shown to capture temperature-dependent trends in the relative stability of polymorphs through estimation of the free energy under the harmonic approximation. By running multiple orders of magnitude faster than DFT, CSP-MACE-Å enables energy and free energy evaluation of far more candidate structures, providing greater confidence when derisking solid forms.

AI.tldr: CSP-MACE-Å is a machine learning interatomic potential that decomposes energy into intramolecular (MACE-POLAR on OMol25) and intermolecular (MACE-POLAR + XDM dispersion + learned delta on 50k B86bPBE-XDM calculations) components. It matches PBE-D3 and approaches B86bPBE-XDM accuracy on CSP benchmark sets, outperforms existing foundation models, captures temperature-dependent polymorph stability via harmonic free energies, and runs orders of magnitude faster than DFT.
AI.motivation: To replace expensive DFT calculations in crystal structure prediction with a fast, accurate machine learning interatomic potential, enabling evaluation of far more candidate structures for solid-form derisking.
AI.method: Decomposes total energy into intramolecular (MACE-POLAR trained on OMol25) and intermolecular parts. Intermolecular combines MACE-POLAR, long-range XDM dispersion, and a learned delta model trained on residuals from 50k B86bPBE-XDM calculations on molecular crystal structures. Reranking uses harmonic free energies.
AI.result: On 19-compound AZ set: comparable to PBE+Neumann-Perrin. On 28-compound blind test set: close to B86bPBE-XDM. Outperforms MACE-POLAR-1 and UMA-OMC. Captures temperature-dependent polymorph stability trends. Harmonic free-energy reranking improves over energy-only ranking.
AI.conclusion: CSP-MACE-Å achieves DFT-level accuracy for CSP at orders-of-magnitude lower computational cost, enabling more thorough exploration of candidate structures and greater confidence in solid-form derisking.

title: Universal response of Rydberg manifolds to standing light waves from the microwave to the X-ray regime
summary: Standing light waves structure the electronic density of a Rydberg atom in a rich but surprisingly systematic fashion. We uncover these systematics, which are nearly universal across a large range of principal quantum numbers n, by varying the wavelength of the standing light over several orders of magnitude. Thereby, we identify five qualitatively different regimes and give their transition criteria in terms of specific critical wavelengths. The bandwidth of the lattice spectrum, manifested in the difference of energies between the states on the edges of the degeneracy-lifted n-manifolds, as well as the organization of the electron density in coordinate and momentum space are used to rationalize the systematics. A experimental setup is proposed to measure the features in the different regimes.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically studies how standing light waves structure the electronic density of Rydberg atoms, identifying five distinct regimes based on critical wavelengths, with analysis of bandwidth and density organization in both coordinate and momentum space, along with an experimental proposal.
AI.motivation: To uncover the systematic and nearly universal structuring of Rydberg atom electron density by standing light waves across a large range of principal quantum numbers.
AI.method: Varying the standing light wavelength over several orders of magnitude and analyzing the lattice spectrum bandwidth (energy differences between degeneracy-lifted n-manifold edge states) and electron density organization in coordinate and momentum space.
AI.result: Five qualitatively different regimes are identified with transition criteria given by specific critical wavelengths.
AI.conclusion: The systematics of standing light wave structuring of Rydberg atoms are nearly universal across a large range of n, and an experimental setup is proposed to measure the features in the different regimes.

title: Geometry-based Discovery of Calcium Battery Cathodes Accelerated by Foundational Machine-Learned Models
summary: Calcium batteries (CBs) are an attractive post-Li-ion technology, offering the appeal of Ca's natural abundance and high volumetric energy density. However, practical realization of CBs remains limited by the scarcity of positive electrode (cathode) materials that support reversible Ca$^{2+}$ (de)intercalation under electrochemical conditions. To address this challenge, we screen the materials project (MP) database for novel host structures that can intercalate Ca using geometry- and chemistry-based design principles. Specifically, we employ the Voronoi polyhedral volume as a descriptor of site compatibility for hosting Ca in potential frameworks. Further, we down-select candidate structures progressively through criteria including charge neutrality, absence of non-Ca mobile cations, thermodynamic (meta)stability, average voltage, and Ca migration barriers ($E_m$) using foundational machine-learning (ML) models. Subsequently, we validate the ensemble-ML-predicted $E_m$ in a subset of the final candidates using density functional theory based nudged elastic band calculations. Overall, from an initial pool of 52,945 MP structures, our workflow identifies 37 promising Ca cathode candidates, several of which exhibit favorable combinations of thermodynamic (meta)stability, voltage, and Ca-mobility, marking them as strong candidates for synthesis and electrochemical characterization. Particularly, we identify two Ca cathode candidates with markedly low Ca$^{2+}~E_m$ (CaSc$_2$V$_2$O$_8$ and CaVSO$_4$F$_3$), and four cathode candidates with thermodynamically stable charged states (Ca$_3$(CoO$_2$)$_4$, Ca$_3$Mn$_4$(TeO$_6$)$_2$, CaVF$_5$, and CaVSO$_4$F$_3$). Beyond identifying Ca-cathodes, our work establishes geometry-based descriptors and ML-based workflows as transferable methods for high-throughput screening, enabling the rapid discovery of novel materials for battery and other applications.

AI.tldr: This study screens 52,945 structures from the Materials Project database using geometry-based descriptors (Voronoi polyhedral volume) and machine learning to identify 37 promising Ca-cathode candidates for calcium batteries, with two showing notably low Ca²⁺ migration barriers and four exhibiting thermodynamically stable charged states.
AI.motivation: Calcium batteries are attractive for post-Li-ion technology due to Ca's natural abundance and high volumetric energy density, but practical realization is limited by scarcity of cathode materials that support reversible Ca²⁺ (de)intercalation.
AI.method: Screened Materials Project database using Voronoi polyhedral volume as a site-compatibility descriptor; applied progressive down-selection via charge neutrality, absence of non-Ca mobile cations, thermodynamic (meta)stability, average voltage, and ML-predicted Ca migration barriers; validated a subset with DFT-based nudged elastic band calculations.
AI.result: From 52,945 initial structures, 37 promising Ca cathode candidates were identified. Two candidates (CaSc₂V₂O₈ and CaVSO₄F₃) exhibit markedly low Ca²⁺ migration barriers, and four (Ca₃(CoO₂)₄, Ca₃Mn₄(TeO₆)₂, CaVF₅, CaVSO₄F₃) have thermodynamically stable charged states.
AI.conclusion: Establishes geometry-based descriptors and ML-based workflows as transferable high-throughput screening methods for rapid discovery of novel battery materials and other applications.

title: Comment on "Spin-1/2 Kagome Heisenberg Antiferromagnet: Machine Learning Discovery of the Spinon Pair-Density-Wave Ground State"
summary: A recent article [Phys. Rev. X 15, 011047 (2025)] utilizes group-equivariant convolutional neural networks to study the ground state of the kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet. On the largest finite-size cluster studied to date ($N=108$), the authors report variational energies significantly lower than other numerical methods, including state-of-the-art density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations. In contrast to previous results suggesting a possible spin-liquid ground state, the authors observe a spinon pair-density-wave ground state. We find that: (i) the reported low energies are artifacts of broken ergodicity in the Metropolis--Hastings sampling, since the single-spin-flip update rule utilized by the authors effectively freezes the Markov chains; and (ii) when ergodic sampling is enforced via spin-exchange updates, the neural network converges to energies significantly higher than existing DMRG results, calling the paper's claims into question.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies critical flaws in a recent neural network study of the kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet, showing that reported low variational energies were due to broken ergodicity from single-spin-flip Metropolis-Hastings sampling, and that proper sampling yields energies higher than DMRG results.
AI.motivation: To critically examine and verify the claims made in Phys. Rev. X 15, 011047 (2025), which used group-equivariant CNNs to study the kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet and reported variational energies significantly lower than other methods, suggesting a spinon pair-density-wave ground state contrary to previous spin-liquid indications.
AI.method: The authors re-evaluate the neural network approach by examining the Metropolis-Hastings sampling procedure, specifically testing the ergodicity of single-spin-flip update rules versus spin-exchange updates, and comparing variational energies against DMRG results.
AI.result: (i) The low reported energies are artifacts of broken ergodicity because single-spin-flip updates freeze Markov chains; (ii) when ergodic sampling via spin-exchange updates is used, the neural network converges to energies significantly higher than existing DMRG results, invalidating the original paper's claims.
AI.conclusion: The claims of the original paper are called into question; the apparent low-energy ground state is attributable to sampling artifacts rather than genuine physics.

title: Inverse generalised spin models of answers to questionnaires
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures (plus 28 pages and 7 figures in the appendices)
summary: Network psychometrics conceptualises psychological constructs as emergent properties of systems of interacting variables. Energy-based probabilistic models have gained popularity as models of these interactions, but their psychometric application has so far been limited, since most implementations assume binary or ternary responses and rely on limiting inference assumptions. We infer and analyse three generalised spin models of ordinal questionnaire data: the generalised Ising, Blume-Capel (BC), and Blume-Emery-Griffiths (BEG) models. We prove the concavity of the maximum likelihood estimation of the parameters, as well as the gauge invariance of the Ising and BC models. Afterwards, we propose an inference protocol of approximated likelihood maximisation, based on the Monte Carlo estimation of the likelihood gradients. We apply this procedure to eleven psychometric and sociological questionnaires, comparing the inferred spin models against the multivariate Gaussian. We then assess whether the inferred models reproduce the empirical features of the data in terms of principal-component histograms, and histograms of Euclidean and Mahalanobis distances to the mean answer. The multi-modality observed in the histograms of principal components is partially captured by the spin models. This trait of polarisation can be understood, in the light of mean-field theory, as coexistence of stable and metastable phases of the spin models. The BEG model systematically outperforms the other models in capturing the distribution of distances to the mean, while all models underestimate the heavy tails of the Mahalanobis distance. Overall, the analysis witnesses the predictive power of the BEG model, able to account better than others for the abundance of outliers and mean responders, and reveals highly non-linear features of questionnaire data that both Gaussian and spin models fail to account for.

AI.tldr: The paper infers three generalised spin models (Ising, Blume-Capel, Blume-Emery-Griffiths) for ordinal questionnaire data in network psychometrics, proves concavity of MLE and gauge invariance, proposes an inference protocol via Monte Carlo likelihood maximisation, and applies it to 11 datasets. The BEG model outperforms others in capturing distance distributions, though all models underestimate heavy tails of Mahalanobis distance.
AI.motivation: Energy-based probabilistic models have gained popularity for modelling psychological constructs as interacting variables, but their psychometric application has been limited due to assumptions of binary/ternary responses and restrictive inference methods. The authors aim to extend these models to ordinal questionnaire data.
AI.method: The authors generalise three spin models (Ising, Blume-Capel, Blume-Emery-Griffiths) to ordinal data, prove concavity of maximum likelihood estimation and gauge invariance for Ising and BC models, and develop a Monte Carlo-based approximated likelihood maximisation inference protocol. They apply this to 11 psychometric/sociological questionnaires and compare against the multivariate Gaussian model.
AI.result: The BEG model systematically outperforms others in capturing distributions of distances to the mean. Multi-modality in principal-component histograms (polarisation) is partially captured by spin models and explained via mean-field theory as coexistence of stable/metastable phases. All models underestimate heavy tails of the Mahalanobis distance.
AI.conclusion: The BEG model demonstrates superior predictive power for outlier and mean-responder patterns in questionnaire data. However, highly non-linear features remain that neither Gaussian nor spin models adequately capture, indicating room for further model development.

title: More than just light management -- The multiple advantages of nano- and micro-textures in perovskite solar cells
summary: Perovskite-based solar cells have undergone rapid improvements over the last decade enabling highest power conversion efficiencies of single-junction and multi-junction devices. The implementation of nano- or micro-textures has played a major role in this development due to their ability to minimize reflection losses, maximize light trapping, and hence increase light harvesting in the active layer. In the slipstream of these advances, it has become apparent that nano- and micro-textures can also have many other collateral benefits beyond light management. In this article, very recently reported texture-related benefits for perovskite-based solar cells different from light management are reviewed. These are namely (1) improved film wetting from perovskite-solution, (2) enhanced perovskite crystallinity in terms of grain size, crystal orientation and phase homogeneity, (3) enhanced carrier extraction leading to higher open-circuit voltages, and potentially (4) increased mechanical stability upon bending in flexible devices and reduced residual stress. This survey helps to understand textures as a holistic concept to further improve perovskite-based solar cells, photodetectors and light emitting diodes.

AI.tldr: This review examines non-optical benefits of nano/micro-textures in perovskite solar cells, including improved film wetting, enhanced crystallinity, better carrier extraction, and increased mechanical stability.
AI.motivation: While textures were initially used for light management (anti-reflection and light trapping) in perovskite solar cells, recent studies reveal additional collateral benefits. This review aims to systematically catalog these overlooked advantages beyond photonic effects.
AI.method: The authors survey recent literature on texture-related benefits in perovskite-based solar cells, categorizing four main areas: (1) film wetting from perovskite solution, (2) crystallinity (grain size, orientation, phase homogeneity), (3) carrier extraction and open-circuit voltage enhancement, and (4) mechanical stability and residual stress reduction.
AI.result: Textures improve perovskite solution spreading/wetting, promote larger grains and better crystal orientation, enhance carrier extraction leading to higher Voc, and improve mechanical flexibility while reducing residual stress in devices.
AI.conclusion: Nano/micro-textures should be understood as a holistic design concept for perovskite optoelectronics (solar cells, photodetectors, LEDs), offering benefits that extend well beyond traditional light management.

title: Geometry and localization: Probing Localization Landscape Theory on the Bethe Lattice
comment: 50 pages, 13 figures. arXiv admin note: substantial text overlap with arXiv:2512.04037
summary: The Localization Landscape Theory (LLT) offers a classical analogy for understanding Anderson localization through an effective confining potential, whose percolation threshold has been proposed to mark the mobility edge. While this correspondence shows striking numerical agreement in three dimensions, its theoretical foundations remain an open question. In this work, we extend the analysis of the LLT on the Bethe lattice presented in~\cite{Tonetti2026}. In this setting in both the Anderson localization transition and the LLT percolation problem admit exact solutions. Our analysis reveals that the two transitions are distinct, with markedly different critical behaviors. Notably, the LLT percolation transition falls into the standard mean-field universality class, in sharp contrast with the unconventional critical behavior of the Anderson transition on the Bethe lattice. Nonetheless, the LLT framework reproduces several exact results, capturing nontrivial features of the very low-disorder regime: it predicts the position of the isolated eigenvalue, the minimal disorder at which both the LLT percolation curve and the mobility edge first appear, and the Aizenman--Warzel lower bound for localization. We also study the dependence of the LLT percolation threshold on the energy shift, evaluate the LLT prediction for the Density of States, and derive several results on the statistical properties of the variables controlling the problem. Finally, we develop an extreme-value analysis showing that the LLT prediction for the Density of States overestimates the amplitude of the tails close to the boundary of the continuous spectrum. These findings provide an exact analytical benchmark showing that, despite its geometric appeal, the LLT does not generally reproduce the quantum critical properties of Anderson localization, while still offering a powerful tool to understand its very low-disorder regime.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the analysis of the Localization Landscape Theory (LLT) on the Bethe lattice, where both Anderson localization and LLT percolation admit exact solutions. It shows the two transitions are distinct with different critical behaviors—LLT falls into standard mean-field universality while Anderson transition does not—but LLT still reproduces several exact results in the very low-disorder regime, including the isolated eigenvalue position, minimal disorder for mobility edge appearance, and the Aizenman-Warzel lower bound.
AI.motivation: To resolve the theoretical foundations of the Localization Landscape Theory (LLT) and determine whether its percolation threshold genuinely corresponds to the Anderson mobility edge, especially given the striking numerical agreement in 3D but lack of theoretical clarity.
AI.method: Extension of LLT analysis to the Bethe lattice, where both the Anderson localization transition and the LLT percolation problem are exactly solvable. The study includes analysis of critical behavior, dependence of percolation threshold on energy shift, Density of States predictions, statistical properties of controlling variables, and extreme-value analysis of the DOS tails.
AI.result: The two transitions are distinct with markedly different critical behaviors: LLT percolation belongs to the standard mean-field universality class, contrasting with the unconventional critical behavior of the Anderson transition on the Bethe lattice. Despite this, LLT reproduces the isolated eigenvalue position, the minimal disorder for mobility edge appearance, and the Aizenman-Warzel lower bound. The LLT prediction for the DOS overestimates the tail amplitude near the continuous spectrum boundary.
AI.conclusion: Despite its geometric appeal and numerical agreement in 3D, the LLT does not generally reproduce the quantum critical properties of Anderson localization. However, it remains a powerful tool for understanding the very low-disorder regime.

title: Records, drift, and the longest increasing subsequence of biased Gaussian random walks
summary: The longest increasing subsequence (LIS) of a random walk has so far been studied mainly for zero-mean, symmetric step increments. We numerically investigate the LIS of biased Gaussian random walks, with unit-variance increments and positive drift $μ_{p} = Φ^{-1}(p)$, where $p = \mathbb{P}(ξ>0)$. In contrast with the symmetric case, we find that for every fixed $p>1/2$ the mean LIS length grows linearly, $\langle L_{n}(p)\rangle \sim a(p)n$, with $a(p)$ increasing from $0$ at $p=1/2$ to $1$ as $p \to 1$. The record count is also linear, with coefficient $λ(p)$ given by Spitzer's formula for the mean ascending ladder epoch, and the LIS becomes increasingly aligned with this record skeleton as $p$ grows. At the symmetric point $p=1/2$, the record skeleton collapses to the Sparre Andersen $\sqrt{n}$ scale, while the LIS returns to the symmetric finite-variance $\sqrt{n}\log{n}$ regime. Near this limit, the excess $a(μ_{p})-λ(μ_{p})$ vanishes more slowly than linearly in the drift, although our data do not resolve a single power law. The empirical distribution of $L_{n}$ also changes across the singular point, from lognormal-like at $p=1/2$ to fluctuations consistent with Gaussian behavior for every sampled $p>1/2$.

AI.tldr: This paper numerically investigates the longest increasing subsequence (LIS) of biased Gaussian random walks with positive drift. It finds that for p>1/2, mean LIS length grows linearly with n (coefficient a(p) increasing from 0 to 1), record count also grows linearly (coefficient λ(p) from Spitzer's formula), and the LIS aligns with the record skeleton. At the symmetric point p=1/2, the behavior reverts to known sublinear scaling (√n log n). The excess a(p)-λ(p) vanishes slowly near the symmetric limit, and the distribution transitions from lognormal-like (p=1/2) to Gaussian (p>1/2).
AI.motivation: Prior work on LIS of random walks focused mainly on zero-mean, symmetric steps. This paper extends the investigation to biased (positive drift) Gaussian random walks to understand how asymmetry changes the scaling behavior of LIS length.
AI.method: Numerical simulation of biased Gaussian random walks with unit-variance increments and positive drift μ_p = Φ^{-1}(p), where p = ℙ(ξ>0). The mean LIS length, record count, and their distributions are computed for various p>1/2 and compared to the symmetric case p=1/2.
AI.result: For p>1/2, mean LIS length grows linearly: ⟨L_n(p)⟩ ∼ a(p)n, with a(p) increasing from 0 to 1 as p→1. Record count also linear with coefficient λ(p) from Spitzer's formula. At p=1/2, LIS reverts to √n log n scaling. The excess a(p)-λ(p) vanishes slowly near p=1/2, and the distribution transitions from lognormal-like (p=1/2) to Gaussian (p>1/2).
AI.conclusion: Biased random walks exhibit a singular transition at p=1/2: for any drift, LIS length becomes linear in n, aligning with the record skeleton, while the symmetric case shows sublinear scaling. The transition region shows complex behavior not captured by a single power law.

title: Helimagnetic Josephson diode effect
summary: We study the Josephson diode effect in the one-dimensional superconductor/helimagnet/superconductor junctions using the Green's function method. For the spin-singlet $s$-wave pairing in superconductors, it is found that the necessary conditions for the Josephson diode effect are the nonzero chemical potential and the conical magnetic configuration in the helimagnet. The diode efficiency is strongly dependent on the chemical potential, chirality, tilt angle and exchange coupling in the helimagnet. The high efficiency close to $40\%$ can be obtained for specific parameter values. The sign of the diode efficiency can be tuned by changing the chirality, tilt angle, exchange coupling and chemical potential. The dependence of the diode efficiency on the number of supercells in the helimagnet is also investigated. The characteristics of the supercurrent nonreciprocity and diode efficiency in the junctions are clarified through the symmetry analysis and the energy band calculations. The diode effect for the spin-triplet $p$-wave pairing in superconductors is also discussed and the nonzero chemical potential is no longer a necessary condition for the Josephson diode effect due to the equal-spin Cooper pair-mediated transport in the $p$-wave junctions. These results provide a scheme for the Josephson diode effect without spin-orbit coupling, which possesses the potential applications in the design of dissipationless electronic devices.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically investigates the Josephson diode effect in superconductor/helimagnet/superconductor junctions, showing that nonzero chemical potential and conical magnetic configuration are necessary for s-wave superconductors, while p-wave junctions relax this condition due to equal-spin Cooper pair transport, achieving up to ~40% diode efficiency tunable by multiple parameters.
AI.motivation: To study the Josephson diode effect in one-dimensional superconductor/helimagnet/superconductor junctions and identify necessary conditions and mechanisms for the effect without spin-orbit coupling.
AI.method: Green's function method for theoretical analysis; symmetry analysis and energy band calculations to characterize supercurrent nonreciprocity and diode efficiency.
AI.result: Nonzero chemical potential and conical magnetic configuration are necessary for Josephson diode effect in s-wave junctions; diode efficiency up to ~40% can be achieved; efficiency sign tunable by chirality, tilt angle, exchange coupling, and chemical potential; for p-wave junctions, nonzero chemical potential is not necessary due to equal-spin Cooper pair transport.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a scheme for realizing the Josephson diode effect without spin-orbit coupling, with potential applications in dissipationless electronic devices.

title: Reinterpreting Memory Effects in Nonequilibrium Systems: From Temporal Dynamics to Steady-State Signatures via NEGF
summary: We investigate memory effects and quantum transport in two-dimensional lattice systems within the framework of non-equilibrium Green's functions and Schwinger-Keldysh non-equilibrium quantum field theory. Starting from a 2D tight-binding Hamiltonian, we employ the Dyson expansion on the Keldysh contour and the second-order Born and self-consistent Born Approximation to derive the electronic self-energies associated with elastic and inelastic scattering mechanisms.Static disorder produces a local self-energy and a rapidly decaying memory kernel, characteristic of Markovian dynamics, whereas electron-phonon coupling generates temporally nonlocal self-energies and genuine Non-Markovian behavior. We demonstrate that these distinct memory signatures are directly reflected in the spectral function, which we propose as a diagnostic probe of non-equilibrium memory effects. Further we explore 1PI and 2PI effective actions to see their memory perspectives studying their coarse-graining behavior. Building on this theoretical framework, we further apply the conventional NEGF formalism to two paradigmatic two-dimensional models-the Hofstadter and an RKKY-coupled system to explore how different microscopic Hamiltonians influence Markovian and Non-Markovian nature. Our results provide a unified connection between scattering mechanisms, memory effects, and quantum transport in low-dimensional systems.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates memory effects in 2D lattice systems using non-equilibrium Green's functions and Schwinger-Keldysh theory, showing that static disorder yields Markovian dynamics while electron-phonon coupling produces Non-Markovian behavior, with spectral functions serving as diagnostic probes. The framework is applied to Hofstadter and RKKY-coupled models.
AI.motivation: To understand how different scattering mechanisms (static disorder vs. electron-phonon coupling) influence memory effects in quantum transport within 2D lattice systems, and to establish a unified theoretical connection between scattering mechanisms, memory effects, and transport properties.
AI.method: The authors employ non-equilibrium Green's functions (NEGF) and Schwinger-Keldysh quantum field theory starting from a 2D tight-binding Hamiltonian. They use Dyson expansion on the Keldysh contour with second-order Born and self-consistent Born approximations to derive self-energies. They also explore 1PI and 2PI effective actions to study coarse-graining behavior.
AI.result: Static disorder yields local self-energies and rapidly decaying memory kernels (Markovian dynamics), while electron-phonon coupling generates temporally nonlocal self-energies (Non-Markovian behavior). These memory signatures are reflected in the spectral function. Application to Hofstadter and RKKY-coupled models reveals how different Hamiltonians influence Markovian/Non-Markovian nature.
AI.conclusion: The spectral function can serve as a diagnostic probe of non-equilibrium memory effects, and the framework provides a unified connection between scattering mechanisms, memory effects, and quantum transport in low-dimensional systems.

title: How Atoms Interact Within Molecules
summary: Fundamental understanding of interatomic forces in molecules must emerge from quantum mechanics, yet widely used empirical force fields rely on simplified mechanistic approximations that often fail to capture the complexity of many-body systems. Here we employ recent developments in quantum field theory (QFT) for long-range electron correlation and machine learning force fields (MLFFs) to directly compute the depth and scatter of interatomic forces for molecular systems containing hundreds of atoms. We find that while the average interaction strength decays polynomially with interatomic separation, the interaction scatter remains robust and exhibits substantial anisotropy. Both QFT and MLFFs demonstrate that increasing the molecular size further amplifies this scatter and anisotropy -- a phenomenon not considered in traditional textbook empirical models. These results provide new benchmarks for force models, shift the focus from interacting atoms to interacting ``hotspots'' that might determine the folding pathways of (bio)polymers, and rationalize why MLFFs are uniquely successful in capturing the nuances of complex molecular systems. Our findings offer a roadmap for the development of more accurate and quantum-aware molecular force fields.

AI.tldr: Using QFT and MLFFs, the authors show that interatomic forces exhibit robust, anisotropic scatter that amplifies with molecular size—challenging traditional empirical force fields and suggesting that interactions occur via "hotspots" rather than uniform pairwise potentials.
AI.motivation: Empirical force fields rely on simplified mechanistic approximations that fail to capture the complexity of many-body systems; a fundamental quantum-mechanical understanding of interatomic forces is needed to improve molecular modeling.
AI.method: The study employs quantum field theory (QFT) for long-range electron correlation and machine learning force fields (MLFFs) to compute the depth and scatter of interatomic forces in molecular systems with hundreds of atoms.
AI.result: Average interaction strength decays polynomially with distance, but interaction scatter remains robust and substantially anisotropic. Increasing molecular size amplifies both scatter and anisotropy—an effect absent in traditional empirical models.
AI.conclusion: The findings shift the focus from interacting atoms to interacting "hotspots" that may determine folding pathways of (bio)polymers, rationalize MLFF success, and provide a roadmap for developing more accurate, quantum-aware molecular force fields.

title: Lingering Sweetness of Ethanol Clusters: Sensory Discovery and Objective Discrimination by Impedance-Based Electronic Tongue
summary: Ethanol is conventionally perceived only as a pungent tastant, while the potential sweet properties of ethanol clusters have remained unrecognized. Here we show that ethanol tetramers exhibit a unique time dependent lingering sweetness, distinct from the immediate upupfront sweetness of conventional sweeteners. To objectively verify this phenomenon, we developed an impedance based bionic electronic tongue that monitors changes at a lipid polymer membrane interface. Sensory evaluation revealed increasing ethanol cluster content from 4.83% to 29.53% prolonged sweetness duration from 10s to 25s, whereas sweetness intensity remained low to moderate (1.0-1.7 on a 10 point scale). Using this electronic tongue, we achieved objective discrimination between upfront and lingering sweetness,full band phase angle scanning identified optimal frequencies of 0.933Hz (t=0.171s) for xylitol (fast binding and dissociation) and 0.03Hz (t=5.305s) for ethanol clusters (slow binding and dissociation). Phase angle responses correlated strongly with sensory sweetness duration. In natural aged Chinese Baijiu (1-20 years), low frequency phase angle signals positively correlated with sensory lingering sweetness scores, confirming that ethanol cluster accumulation during aging underpins the sweetness of Baijiu. This work expands the classic AH-B sweetness theory from single molecules to supramolecular clusters and provides an analytical platform for probing the temporal dimension of flavor perception.

AI.tldr: Ethanol tetramers exhibit a unique lingering sweetness, distinct from conventional upfront sweeteners. Using an impedance-based bionic electronic tongue, the study shows that ethanol cluster content correlates with sweetness duration, and phase angle scanning enables objective discrimination between fast (xylitol) and slow (ethanol clusters) binding kinetics. This work extends the AH-B sweetness theory from single molecules to supramolecular clusters.
AI.motivation: To challenge the conventional view that ethanol is only a pungent tastant by revealing the unrecognized sweet properties of ethanol clusters, and to provide an objective analytical platform for probing the temporal dimension of flavor perception.
AI.method: Developed an impedance-based bionic electronic tongue with a lipid polymer membrane interface; used full-band phase angle scanning to identify optimal frequencies for different sweeteners; conducted sensory evaluation of ethanol cluster solutions and naturally aged Chinese Baijiu (1-20 years).
AI.result: Ethanol cluster content increase from 4.83% to 29.53% prolonged sweetness duration from 10s to 25s (intensity 1.0-1.7/10). Optimal frequencies: 0.933 Hz for xylitol (fast), 0.03 Hz for ethanol clusters (slow). Low-frequency phase angle signals positively correlated with sensory lingering sweetness scores in aged Baijiu.
AI.conclusion: Ethanol clusters (tetramers) produce time-dependent lingering sweetness, expanding the classic AH-B sweetness theory from single molecules to supramolecular clusters. The bionic electronic tongue enables objective discrimination between upfront and lingering sweetness.

title: Field-Driven Hybrid Filament Formation Governs Switching in Ta-HfO$_2$-Pt Memristors
summary: Memristive devices have gained significant attention for their potential in next-generation non-volatile memory and neuromorphic computing architectures. Among emerging candidates, transition metal oxides have proven particularly promising. While the switching mechanism in Ta/HfO$_2$/Pt devices was long attributed solely to oxygen vacancy based filaments, recent experimental evidence suggests a more complex dual-regime: the diffusion of metal cations also contributes to the formation of a conductive bridge. However, the precise atomistic mechanisms governing this metal cation migration remain poorly understood. Additionally, the role of defects such as oxygen vacancies present in the transition metal oxide in determining the final filament size and shape is also not well understood. Here, we employ molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with dynamic charge transfer to provide a detailed analysis of the atomistic mechanisms governing the co-formation of Ta-cation and oxygen-deficient filaments. We clearly show how varying the initial oxygen vacancy concentrations and spatial configurations within the HfO$_2$ matrix influences the final morphology and dimensions of the conductive filament. The switching is governed by field-driven formation and rupture of a hybrid Ta-cation-rich, oxygen-deficient filament in HfO$_2$. Our simulations closely match experiment, validating the model as a robust framework for understanding switching in oxide memristors and guiding designs that reduce cycle-to-cycle and device-to-device variability -- key barriers to high-performance devices.

AI.tldr: This paper uses molecular dynamics simulations with dynamic charge transfer to investigate the co-formation of Ta-cation and oxygen-deficient filaments in Ta/HfO₂/Pt memristive devices, showing how oxygen vacancy concentration and spatial configuration influence filament morphology, and validating the model against experimental data.
AI.motivation: While Ta/HfO₂/Pt devices were thought to switch solely via oxygen vacancy filaments, recent evidence suggests a dual-regime involving metal cation diffusion. However, the atomistic mechanisms of metal cation migration and the role of oxygen vacancies in determining filament size/shape remain poorly understood.
AI.method: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with dynamic charge transfer, varying initial oxygen vacancy concentrations and spatial configurations within the HfO₂ matrix.
AI.result: The simulations reveal field-driven formation and rupture of hybrid Ta-cation-rich, oxygen-deficient filaments, with filament morphology and dimensions strongly dependent on the initial oxygen vacancy distribution.
AI.conclusion: The model closely matches experimental results, providing a robust framework for understanding switching in oxide memristors and guiding designs to reduce cycle-to-cycle and device-to-device variability.

title: Improving CFT Operators Using Machine Learning
summary: Finite-size effects limit the accuracy with which conformal data can be extracted from lattice simulations of critical systems. While action improvement suppresses some corrections to scaling, it does not address operator-dependent effects arising from imperfect lattice representations of continuum conformal fields. In this work, we propose a data-driven method for improving lattice operators themselves, constructing estimators with enhanced overlap with the corresponding primary operators of the continuum conformal field theory. We identify improved lattice representations of leading spin and energy operators in three two-dimensional critical systems: the Ising model, the q = 3 Potts model, and the dilute q = 3 Potts model. In all cases, the resulting operators exhibit reduced corrections to scaling and yield more accurate estimates of scaling dimensions compared to conventional lattice choices. The code and analysis workflows used to produce these results are made available in an accompanying GitHub repository.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a data-driven method to improve lattice operators in critical systems, reducing finite-size effects and yielding more accurate estimates of scaling dimensions, demonstrated on the Ising model, q=3 Potts model, and dilute q=3 Potts model.
AI.motivation: Finite-size effects in lattice simulations of critical systems limit the accuracy of extracted conformal data; action improvement alone does not address operator-dependent imperfections from lattice representations of continuum conformal fields.
AI.method: A data-driven method is introduced to construct improved lattice operators with enhanced overlap with continuum primary operators, applied to leading spin and energy operators in three 2D critical systems.
AI.result: Improved operators exhibit reduced corrections to scaling and yield more accurate estimates of scaling dimensions compared to conventional lattice choices across all three tested models.
AI.conclusion: Data-driven operator improvement can effectively mitigate finite-size effects in lattice simulations of critical systems; code and workflows are publicly available.

title: Revealing quantum metric multipoles in magnetic topological insulator MnBi2Te4
summary: Nonlinear electronic transport has emerged as a powerful probe of the quantum geometry in topological quantum materials, where the band topology and broken symmetries facilitate power law current voltage responses beyond Ohms law. While nonlinear transport of the second and third orders has been studied in several quantum materials, higher-order transport has so far mainly remained experimentally inaccessible, leaving more detailed features of the quantum geometry unexplored. Here, we observe higher order nonlinear electronic transport up to the seventh harmonic order in multilayer magnetic topological insulator MnBi2Te4. We find an even-odd behavior where the odd order nonlinear transport components dominate while the even-order ones are suppressed. Temperature and magnetic field dependent measurements show a strong correlation between the nonlinear transport and the magnetic phases of MnBi2Te4. Through scaling analysis and theoretical calculations, quantum metric multipoles and nonlinear Drude conductivities are identified as the microscopic origins of the nonlinear transport.

AI.tldr: The paper reports observation of higher-order nonlinear electronic transport up to the 7th harmonic in multilayer MnBi₂Te₄, revealing odd-order dominance, magnetic phase correlation, and quantum metric multipoles as microscopic origins.
AI.motivation: Higher-order nonlinear transport beyond 2nd and 3rd orders has remained experimentally inaccessible, leaving detailed quantum geometry features unexplored.
AI.method: Nonlinear transport measurements up to 7th harmonic order in multilayer MnBi₂Te₄, combined with temperature and magnetic field dependent measurements, scaling analysis, and theoretical calculations.
AI.result: Observed higher-order nonlinear transport up to the 7th harmonic; odd-order components dominate while even-order ones are suppressed; strong correlation between nonlinear transport and magnetic phases of MnBi₂Te₄.
AI.conclusion: Quantum metric multipoles and nonlinear Drude conductivities are identified as the microscopic origins of the observed higher-order nonlinear transport.

title: Enhanced Density Fluctuations Near a Disordered Chiral Topological Transition
summary: The universal statistics of density fluctuations of localized quantum states may offer unprecedented opportunities to probe and understand quantum transport in connection with dimensionality, coherence, symmetry and disorder. To date, the possible role of topological phase transitions in the fluctuation statistics is not studied yet. Using a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain subject to off-diagonal disorder (so that chiral symmetry is preserved), this work investigates how a disorder driven topological phase transition impacts on the spatial fluctuations of the logarithmic wave-packet density $\ln P(r)$ at distance $r$ from the initial excitation. Away from the transition, in both topological and trivial localized phases, the standard deviation follows the conventional one-dimensional scaling $σ[\ln P(r)]\sim r^θ$ with $θ\simeq 1/2$. Near the transition, however, the fluctuation growth is enhanced: the fitted exponent $θ$ increases above $1/2$ in a nonmonotonic manner before returning close to $1/2$ at criticality. We interpret this behavior from the energy-resolved density of states and localization length. Near the transition, several energy sectors carry appreciable spectral weight and exhibit competitive decay rates, preventing a single localization scale from dominating the accessible wave-packet tail and thereby enhancing the fluctuations of $\ln P(r)$. Our results establish wave-packet fluctuation statistics as a dynamical diagnostic of disordered chiral topological transitions and motivate broader studies of fluctuation phenomena in disordered topological quantum systems.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how disorder-driven topological phase transitions affect the spatial fluctuations of logarithmic wave-packet density in a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain with chiral symmetry. Near the transition, fluctuation growth is enhanced due to competing decay rates from multiple energy sectors, while away from it, standard one-dimensional scaling holds.
AI.motivation: To uncover the role of topological phase transitions in the fluctuation statistics of localized quantum states, which has not been studied previously despite the known connection between density fluctuations and quantum transport.
AI.method: Using a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain with off-diagonal disorder (preserving chiral symmetry), the authors study spatial fluctuations of $\ln P(r)$ and extract the scaling exponent $\theta$ from standard deviation $\sigma[\ln P(r)] \sim r^\theta$ across topological, trivial, and critical phases.
AI.result: Away from the transition, $\theta \simeq 1/2$ in both topological and trivial phases. Near the transition, $\theta$ increases above $1/2$ nonmonotonically before returning to ~1/2 at criticality. This enhancement arises from multiple energy sectors with competing decay rates near the transition.
AI.conclusion: Wave-packet fluctuation statistics serve as a dynamical diagnostic of disordered chiral topological transitions, motivating broader studies of fluctuation phenomena in disordered topological quantum systems.

title: Partial Entropy production of active particles with hidden states in potentials
summary: Partially observed stochastic systems can appear (almost) time-reversal symmetric while in fact operating far from equilibrium. The present work extends the perturbative framework introduced in [Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 198302 (2026)] to calculate in a generic confining potential the partial entropy production, which quantifies the time-reversal asymmetry of a generic active particle with hidden self-propulsion. Focusing on the harmonic case, we apply our framework to reproduce an exact result for the partial entropy production rate of an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle and to derive the partial entropy production rate of a run-and-tumble particle.

AI.tldr: This paper extends a perturbative framework to calculate partial entropy production (time-reversal asymmetry) for active particles with hidden self-propulsion in confining potentials, reproducing exact results for active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particles and deriving new results for run-and-tumble particles in harmonic traps.
AI.motivation: Partially observed stochastic systems can appear time-reversal symmetric while actually operating far from equilibrium, motivating the need to quantify hidden irreversibility via partial entropy production.
AI.method: Extends a perturbative framework from [Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 198302 (2026)] to calculate partial entropy production for generic active particles with hidden self-propulsion in generic confining potentials, then applies it to the harmonic case.
AI.result: Reproduces the exact partial entropy production rate for an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle and derives the partial entropy production rate for a run-and-tumble particle in a harmonic potential.
AI.conclusion: The perturbative framework successfully captures time-reversal asymmetry in hidden active systems, validated by exact results for AOUP and extended to RTP dynamics.

title: Effective Theory of Fermion Quartet Condensation
summary: We develop a theory of superconductivity (or superfluidity) based on condensed fermion quartets focusing on the dilute spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ systems at zero temperature. In the spirit of the Bardeen--Cooper--Schrieffer ansatz, a variational wavefunction is constructed such that, within the so-called ``dilute quartet approximation", it is the ground state of an effective quartic Hamiltonian. For a given two-body interaction in favor of quartetting, the gap parameter is suitably defined and the gap equation is also derived. As to the excited states, an intuitive physical picture based on a sixteen-dimensional ``occupation space" is depicted and the associated eigen-energies are obtained. This theory is applied to compute the superfluid fraction, which is found to be the same as in conventional superconductors, despite the interacting nature of the quartet problem.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a theory of superconductivity/superfluidity based on condensed fermion quartets (rather than Cooper pairs), constructing a BCS-like variational wavefunction for dilute spin-1/2 systems, deriving a gap equation, analyzing excited states via a 16-dimensional occupation space, and showing that the superfluid fraction matches that of conventional superconductors.
AI.motivation: To extend BCS theory beyond Cooper pairing to describe superconductivity mediated by fermion quartet condensation, where the fundamental building block is a four-fermion bound state rather than a pair.
AI.method: A BCS-inspired variational wavefunction is constructed for condensed fermion quartets under the dilute quartet approximation, leading to an effective quartic Hamiltonian. A gap parameter is introduced and the corresponding gap equation derived. Excited states are analyzed using a 16-dimensional occupation space.
AI.result: The superfluid fraction computed from this quartet-based theory is identical to that of conventional BCS superconductors, despite the more complex (quartic) interacting nature of the system.
AI.conclusion: Fermion quartet condensation provides a viable theoretical framework for superconductivity/superfluidity, yielding the same superfluid fraction as BCS theory, suggesting universal behavior in the superfluid response regardless of whether the condensate is composed of pairs or quartets.

title: Measuring anyon dispersion with tunneling probes
summary: Anyons are usually characterized by their topological data and their fractional quantum numbers under global symmetries. In lattice systems such as fractional Chern insulators (FCI), they are also mobile quasiparticles. Their motion controls the possible ground states of the dilute anyon gas obtained by doping an FCI, including possible superconducting states. We show how tunneling probes can measure this motion. In scanning tunneling spectroscopy, weak disorder produces spatially oscillating quasiparticle-interference patterns whose branches reveal the dispersion of fractionalized constituents. In quantum twisting microscopy, planar momentum-conserving tunneling selects the total momentum of the injected electron, so the continuum thresholds of fractionalized electron spectra encode the dispersion of the constituent anyons. The resulting spectra distinguish compact electron-like excitations, bound anyon molecules, and unbound anyon continuum.

AI.tldr: This paper shows how tunneling probes (STM and quantum twisting microscopy) can measure the motion and dispersion of anyons in fractional Chern insulators, revealing signatures of fractionalized quasiparticles through quasiparticle interference patterns and momentum-resolved tunneling spectra that distinguish electron-like excitations, anyon molecules, and unbound anyon continua.
AI.motivation: Understanding the motion of anyons in lattice systems like fractional Chern insulators is crucial for determining possible ground states upon doping (e.g., superconducting states), but direct experimental probes of anyon mobility remain challenging.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze two tunneling spectroscopy techniques: (1) scanning tunneling spectroscopy, where weak disorder generates quasiparticle interference patterns whose branches reveal anyon dispersion; (2) quantum twisting microscopy, where planar momentum-conserving tunneling selects total electron momentum, allowing continuum thresholds to encode anyon dispersion.
AI.result: Quasiparticle interference patterns in STM reveal the dispersion of fractionalized constituents. Quantum twisting microscopy spectra distinguish three types of excitations: compact electron-like excitations, bound anyon molecules, and an unbound anyon continuum.
AI.conclusion: Tunneling probes can directly measure the motion of fractionalized anyons in FCIs, providing experimental signatures that differentiate between different excitation types and enabling study of the dilute anyon gas.

title: Isotope shifts and hyperfine splitting of the ${}^{1}S_{0}\rightarrow{}^{3}P_{1}$ transition in zinc
summary: We report laser-induced-fluorescence spectroscopy of the \({}^{1}S_{0}\rightarrow{}^{3}P_{1}\) intercombination transition in neutral zinc at \(307.6~\mathrm{nm}\). Isotope shifts are measured for all stable isotopes with kHz-level precision, improving previous data by about two orders of magnitude. For \(^{67}\mathrm{Zn}\), we resolve the excited-state hyperfine structure and determine \(δν_{\mathrm{COG}}^{67,64}=1085.933(4)~\mathrm{MHz}\), \(A=608.922(1)~\mathrm{MHz}\), and \(B=-18.995(4)~\mathrm{MHz}\).
