The Landau-Lifshitz-Bernoulli (LLBe) model can, by design, directly couple atomic-scale simulations with micromagnetics and output consistent predictions of bulk magnetic properties at finite temperatures, from below to above the material's Curie temperature. The LLBe model is validated against established solvers: MUMAX3 for zero-temperature micromagnetics, and FEMCE for high-temperature classic magnetostatics. We present an application of the LLBe model by simulating Heat-Assisted magnetic recording on a thin magnetic track with local heating, demonstrating the multi-scale finite-temperature capabilities of the LLBe.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a multi-scale finite-temperature micromagnetic model (LLBe) that couples atomic-scale simulations with micromagnetics, accurately reproducing both classic magnetostatics of paramagnets at high temperatures and standard micromagnetics in ferromagnets. Validated against MUMAX3 and FEMCE, it is applied to simulate Heat-Assisted Magnetic Recording.
AI.motivation: To develop a unified model that bridges atomic-scale simulations and micromagnetics for consistent predictions of bulk magnetic properties at finite temperatures ranging from below to above the Curie temperature.
AI.method: The Landau-Lifshitz-Bernoulli (LLBe) model combines the Landau-Lifshitz equation with the Bernoulli differential equation, enabling multi-scale finite-temperature micromagnetic simulations.
AI.result: The LLBe model accurately reproduces classic Maxwell magnetostatics of paramagnets at high temperatures and standard micromagnetics in ferromagnets; validated against MUMAX3 (zero-temperature) and FEMCE (high-temperature).
AI.conclusion: The LLBe model effectively demonstrates multi-scale finite-temperature capabilities, as shown in Heat-Assisted Magnetic Recording simulations on a thin magnetic track with local heating.

title: Field-induced multipolar character in the dipolar ground state of the honeycomb rare-earth chalcohalide NdOF
summary: Field-tunable reconstruction of crystalline electric field (CEF) doublets offers a promising avenue for inducing multipolar character, while its observation in real materials has been little explored so far. Here we establish the honeycomb rare-earth chalcohalide NdOF as such a platform. Raman spectroscopy identifies four CEF excitations at 1.7, 15.6, 19.2, and 80.9~meV, and a Zeeman--CEF analysis reproduces their nonlinear field splitting into seven branches. Magnetization and susceptibility over 0.1--9~T are well described by a CEF model for the total angular momentum $J = 9/2$ manifold, confirming the robustness of the extracted CEF scheme. These results demonstrate a field-driven continuous evolution of the ground-state doublet from dipolar to dipolar-multipolar character, with pressure providing a complementary tuning knob, establishing NdOF as a model system for exploring the controlled induction of multipolar components in rare-earth magnets.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that the honeycomb rare-earth chalcohalide NdOF exhibits field-tunable crystalline electric field (CEF) doublets, with four CEF excitations identified via Raman spectroscopy, enabling continuous evolution from dipolar to dipolar-multipolar ground-state character under magnetic field and pressure.
AI.motivation: Field-tunable reconstruction of CEF doublets offers a promising route to induce multipolar character, but this phenomenon has been little explored in real materials.
AI.method: Raman spectroscopy was used to identify four CEF excitations at 1.7, 15.6, 19.2, and 80.9 meV. Zeeman-CEF analysis reproduced their nonlinear field splitting into seven branches. Magnetization and susceptibility data over 0.1–9 T were analyzed using a CEF model for the J=9/2 manifold.
AI.result: The extracted CEF scheme robustly describes the data, revealing a field-driven continuous evolution of the ground-state doublet from dipolar to dipolar-multipolar character. Pressure provides an additional tuning knob.
AI.conclusion: NdOF is established as a model system for exploring controlled induction of multipolar components in rare-earth magnets.

title: Hidden Ising models from the generalized Yang-Baxter equation
summary: We introduce a one dimensional spin $\frac{1}{2}$ Hamiltonian with multi-site interactions, but still local. The algebra of its Hamiltonian densities resembles that of the transverse field Ising model. Using this fact we show that its spectrum is free-fermionic but with a huge degeneracy for each level. The source of the degeneracy is a set of local conserved quantities that act like a classical background field for the quantum system. The thermodynamics of this system is contrasted with the standard Ising model. At the gapless points in the energy spectrum, we show that this system can be derived from the quantum inverse scattering method adapted to a multi-site generalization of the Yang-Baxter equation as introduced by E. Rowell and Z. Wang. The $R$-matrix is constructed using generators of extraspecial 2-groups. This helps us extract all the conserved charges and lay the framework for a general mechanism to generate such multi-site interaction spin systems that are transverse field Ising models under the hood. A remark on how to obtain P. Fendley's free-fermion in disguise models in this formalism is also included.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a 1D spin-1/2 Hamiltonian with local multi-site interactions, whose spectrum is free-fermionic yet highly degenerate due to local conserved quantities acting as a classical background field. The thermodynamics is contrasted with the standard Ising model, and the system is derived from a multi-site generalization of the Yang-Baxter equation using extraspecial 2-group generators, providing a general framework for generating transverse-field-Ising-like models, including Fendley's free-fermion in disguise models.
AI.motivation: To construct and analyze a new class of exactly solvable spin systems with multi-site interactions that exhibit free-fermionic spectra with large degeneracies, and to develop a general algebraic framework for generating such models via a generalized Yang-Baxter equation.
AI.method: The authors construct a 1D spin-1/2 Hamiltonian with local multi-site interactions whose density algebra mirrors that of the transverse field Ising model. They leverage this algebraic structure to prove the spectrum is free-fermionic with degeneracies arising from local conserved charges. At gapless points, they derive the system using the quantum inverse scattering method adapted to a multi-site generalization of the Yang-Baxter equation, constructing the R-matrix from extraspecial 2-group generators.
AI.result: The Hamiltonian exhibits a free-fermionic spectrum with huge degeneracies per level, originating from local conserved quantities that act like a classical background field. A general mechanism is established for generating multi-site interaction spin systems that are effectively transverse field Ising models. The formalism also reproduces Fendley's free-fermion in disguise models.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a new exactly solvable family of multi-site spin models with rich degeneracy structure, unified under a generalized Yang-Baxter framework, and connects to existing free-fermionic models in disguise.

title: Generation of Bloch Points with Controlled Spin Texture Using Geometrical Boundary Conditions
comment: main manuscript: 15 pages and 5 figures; supplement: 12 pages including 7 figures
summary: Bloch points are three-dimensional topological singularities in magnetization that play a key role in topological transformations of spin textures, such as skyrmion creation or annihilation. While topology often enforces the existence of Bloch points in confined geometries like cylindrical nanowires, deterministic control over their position and magnetic configuration remains challenging. Here we demonstrate the generation of Bloch points with controlled spin texture by engineering geometrical boundary conditions in three-dimensional nanomagnets. By introducing a chirality interface between two three-dimensional double-helix nanowires of opposite handedness, forming a kinked, non-collinear structure, we impose competing topological constraints that uniquely define the magnetization configuration surrounding the Bloch point. A saturating magnetic field nucleates head-to-head or tail-to-tail domain configurations at the chirality interface, producing a Bloch-point domain wall with deterministic polarity, circulation and helicity. This geometrical approach enables full three-dimensional control of Bloch point domain walls allowing deterministic engineering of their spin texture and its selective coupling to current-induced Oersted fields.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates deterministic generation and control of Bloch points—3D topological singularities in magnetization—by engineering chirality interfaces between double-helix nanowires of opposite handedness, enabling full control over Bloch point domain wall polarity, circulation, and helicity.
AI.motivation: While Bloch points are crucial for topological transformations like skyrmion creation/annihilation and are topologically enforced in confined geometries (e.g., cylindrical nanowires), deterministic control over their position and magnetic configuration has remained challenging.
AI.method: A chirality interface is engineered between two 3D double-helix nanowires of opposite handedness, forming a kinked, non-collinear structure. This imposes competing topological constraints that uniquely define the magnetization configuration around the Bloch point. A saturating magnetic field nucleates head-to-head or tail-to-tail domain configurations at the interface.
AI.result: The approach produces Bloch-point domain walls with deterministic polarity, circulation, and helicity. Full 3D control of Bloch point domain walls is achieved, enabling selective coupling to current-induced Oersted fields.
AI.conclusion: Geometric boundary conditions in 3D nanomagnets provide a pathway for deterministic engineering of Bloch point spin textures and their selective manipulation via Oersted fields.

title: Transition metal (group V) doping induced spin and valley polarization in MoS$_2$ monolayer
summary: Doping in two-dimensional materials has emerged as an effective tool for modulating their electronic properties and thereby enabling their multifunctional applications. In this work, we present a first-principles study on induced effective magnetic moment and metallicity in MoS$_2$ monolayer by substitutional doping of group-5 transition metal (TM) elements -- V, Nb and Ta. From our study, we observe that the V doping induces half-metallicity, whereas metallic characteristics are observed in the case of Nb and Ta doping. Moreover, V and Ta-doped MoS$_2$ monolayers are observed to show total induced magnetic moments of 0.922 and 0.624 $μ_{\rm B}$, respectively. Importantly, the combined effects of strong spin-orbit coupling (SOC), broken inversion symmetry, and structural asymmetry is observed to lead to a permanent valley polarization in the V- and Ta-MoS$_2$ systems. In particular, we observed a valley polarization of 121 and 21 meVs for V and Ta-doped MoS$_2$, respectively. Furthermore, an enhanced piezoelectric coefficient for the doped systems is observed compared to pristine MoS$_2$. Notably, the simultaneous presence of half-metallicity, substantial valley polarization, and enhanced piezoelectricity in V-doped MoS$_2$ establishes this system as a promising multifunctional platform for next-generation spintronic, valleytronic, and piezoelectric nanodevices. Overall, our findings provide fundamental insights into engineering coupled spin-valley-mechanical degrees of freedom in two-dimensional materials for advanced quantum and nanoelectronic applications.

AI.tldr: A first-principles study shows that V, Nb, and Ta doping in MoS₂ monolayers induces diverse electronic properties: V doping yields half-metallicity with a magnetic moment of 0.922 μB and valley polarization of 121 meV, while Nb and Ta doping produce metallic behavior and Ta doping gives 0.624 μB magnetic moment and 21 meV valley polarization. Enhanced piezoelectricity is also observed, positioning V-doped MoS₂ as a promising platform for spintronic, valleytronic, and piezoelectric devices.
AI.motivation: To explore how substitutional doping of group-5 transition metals (V, Nb, Ta) in MoS₂ monolayers can modulate electronic properties, induce magnetic moments and valley polarization, and enhance piezoelectricity for multifunctional quantum and nanoelectronic applications.
AI.method: First-principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations incorporating spin-orbit coupling for group-5 TM-doped (V, Nb, Ta) MoS₂ monolayers.
AI.result: V doping induces half-metallicity; Nb and Ta doping induce metallic character. Magnetic moments: 0.922 μB (V) and 0.624 μB (Ta). Valley polarization: 121 meV (V) and 21 meV (Ta). Enhanced piezoelectric coefficients in doped systems vs. pristine MoS₂.
AI.conclusion: V-doped MoS₂ simultaneously exhibits half-metallicity, substantial valley polarization, and enhanced piezoelectricity, making it a promising multifunctional platform for spintronic, valleytronic, and piezoelectric nanodevices. The work provides insights into engineering coupled spin-valley-mechanical degrees of freedom in 2D materials.

title: Slave-rotor theory of correlated altermagnets on the Lieb lattice
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures; Supplemental Material: 8 pages, 1 figure
summary: We investigate the metal-insulator transition driven by the onsite repulsive interaction $U$ in an altermagnetic Hubbard model defined on a Lieb lattice. Using the slave-rotor approach at half filling, we find that the system exhibits a cascade of interaction-driven phase transitions. As $U$ increases, the system evolves from a normal metal to an altermagnetic metal, then to an altermagnetic insulator, and eventually to an altermagnetic Mott insulator characterized by the complete suppression of the quasiparticle weight. These phases are supported by the calculation of the electronic spectral function, which features spin-split bands in both the metallic and insulating regimes. However, the spin splitting becomes substantially suppressed in the Mott insulating phase. Our results suggest that the observation of spin splitting in the spectral function of $d$-wave altermagnets with a Lieb-lattice-like structure may be limited to the weak-to-moderate correlation regime.

AI.tldr: The paper studies a metal-insulator transition in an altermagnetic Hubbard model on a Lieb lattice using the slave-rotor approach, revealing a cascade of phases: normal metal → altermagnetic metal → altermagnetic insulator → altermagnetic Mott insulator, with spin splitting suppressed in the Mott phase.
AI.motivation: To understand how onsite Coulomb repulsion U drives metal-insulator transitions in altermagnetic systems, particularly on a Lieb lattice, and to explore the fate of spin-split bands across correlation regimes.
AI.method: Slave-rotor approach applied to an altermagnetic Hubbard model on a Lieb lattice at half filling.
AI.result: The system undergoes a cascade of phase transitions: normal metal → altermagnetic metal → altermagnetic insulator → altermagnetic Mott insulator. Spin-split bands appear in metallic and insulating regimes but are substantially suppressed in the Mott insulating phase.
AI.conclusion: Spin splitting in d-wave altermagnets with Lieb-lattice-like structure is observable only in the weak-to-moderate correlation regime, and is suppressed in the strongly correlated Mott phase.

title: Supercooling of liquids, as described by the Enskog-Vlasov kinetic equation
summary: A model combining Enskog's collision integral for dense fluids with a Vlasov-style description of the van der Waals force is applied to supercooling. First, the spinodal temperature $T_{s}$ is calculated, at which a liquid becomes unstable to small perturbations and transitions to solid. In particular, it turns out that isochoric cooling allows one to reach a lower temperature than isobaric cooling. Second, the surface tension of a supercooled liquid-vapor interface is shown to diverge at $T_{s}$. The singularity is caused by an oscillatory region emerging on the liquid side of the interface as $T\rightarrow T_{s}$; it develops because the liquid approaches instability, and the interface starts radiating (so far, evanescent) waves. At $T=T_{s}$, the waves cease to be evanescent and the oscillatory region extends to infinity -- hence, the singularity of the surface tension. Since this effect has a clear physical interpretation, it should occur regardless of the model and approximations under which it was obtained. This and the other results of the paper are illustrated using argon and several other fluids.

AI.tldr: A model combining Enskog's collision integral with Vlasov-style van der Waals force is applied to supercooling, calculating spinodal temperature and showing surface tension divergence at Ts due to oscillatory wave emergence at the liquid-vapor interface.
AI.motivation: To understand the behavior of supercooled liquids near the spinodal instability, particularly how cooling conditions affect stability limits and how surface tension behaves as the system approaches the spinodal temperature.
AI.method: A hybrid model combining Enskog's collision integral for dense fluids with a Vlasov-style description of van der Waals forces, applied to isochoric and isobaric cooling scenarios; analysis of spinodal temperature and surface tension divergence.
AI.result: Isochoric cooling reaches lower temperatures than isobaric cooling before instability; surface tension diverges at Ts due to oscillatory region emerging on the liquid side of the interface as T→Ts, with evanescent waves becoming extended at Ts.
AI.conclusion: The surface tension singularity at Ts has a clear physical interpretation and should be model-independent; results are illustrated using argon and other fluids.

title: Electronic Origin of Ferromagnetic Excitations in the Candidate Spin-Triplet Superconductor CeSb2
summary: The origin of quasi-one-dimensional (q1D) ferromagnetic (FM) excitations in the candidate spin-triplet superconductor CeSb$_2$ has remained unclear. Here we report an electronic mechanism for emergent q1D magnetism in the quasi-two-dimensional lattice of CeSb$_2$, revealed by angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES). High-resolution ARPES resolves no spin-density-wave gap on the dispersive Fermi pockets, disfavoring a nesting-driven mechanism for the q1D FM excitations. Instead, resonant ARPES reveals a pronounced selective enhancement of Ce 4$f$ spectral weight on the $C_2$-distributed Fermi pockets aligned with the Ce ladder. This observation signifies band-selective Kondo coupling that generates strongly anisotropic magnetic exchange interactions, which can naturally account for both the q1D ferromagnetic excitations and the competing magnetic orders. Our results identify a band-selective Kondo coupling mechanism for emergent low-dimensional magnetism in correlated $f$-electron systems.

AI.tldr: Using ARPES, the study reveals that quasi-1D ferromagnetic excitations in CeSb₂ arise from band-selective Kondo coupling rather than nesting-driven mechanisms, with Ce 4f spectral weight selectively enhanced on C₂-distributed Fermi pockets aligned with Ce ladders, explaining both the q1D magnetism and competing magnetic orders.
AI.motivation: The origin of quasi-1D ferromagnetic excitations in the candidate spin-triplet superconductor CeSb₂ has remained unclear, motivating the investigation of its electronic mechanism.
AI.method: High-resolution angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and resonant ARPES were used to probe the electronic structure, Fermi pockets, and Ce 4f spectral weight distribution in CeSb₂'s quasi-2D lattice.
AI.result: No spin-density-wave gap was found on dispersive Fermi pockets, ruling out nesting-driven mechanisms. Resonant ARPES showed selective enhancement of Ce 4f spectral weight on C₂-distributed Fermi pockets aligned with the Ce ladder, indicating band-selective Kondo coupling.
AI.conclusion: Band-selective Kondo coupling generates strongly anisotropic magnetic exchange interactions, naturally explaining both the q1D ferromagnetic excitations and competing magnetic orders, identifying a new mechanism for emergent low-dimensional magnetism in correlated f-electron systems.

title: Zeeman Pumping of Higgs Bosons in the Balian--Werthamer State
summary: Based on equations of motion of an SO(5) pseudo-spin, we demonstrate a quantum quench protocol using the magnetic pulse to excite an $\textit{undamped}$ heavy Higgs boson in the Balian--Werthamer superfluid (or superconductor). To achieve that, it is essential to include the dipolar interaction in the effective Hamiltonian and to calculate the ground state self-consistently. The pumped heavy Higgs mode has the twisted angular momentum $J=2$ with the projection $J^{\,}_z=0$ and couples to a well-known light Higgs mode ($J=1$, $J^{\,}_z=0$). The numerical method of 26-point Lebedev quadrature is implemented concretely so as to observe the real-time coupled oscillation.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a quantum quench protocol using magnetic pulses to excite an undamped heavy Higgs boson (J=2, Jz=0) in SO(5) pseudo-spin dynamics of Balian-Werthamer superfluids, requiring dipolar interactions and self-consistent ground state calculations, with coupling to the light Higgs mode (J=1, Jz=0) simulated via 26-point Lebedev quadrature.
AI.motivation: To theoretically demonstrate a protocol for exciting an undamped heavy Higgs mode in Balian-Werthamer superfluids/superconductors using magnetic pulse quantum quenches, incorporating dipolar interactions and self-consistent ground states.
AI.method: Uses equations of motion of an SO(5) pseudo-spin, includes dipolar interaction in the effective Hamiltonian, computes ground state self-consistently, and implements 26-point Lebedev quadrature for numerical real-time simulation of coupled oscillations.
AI.result: Successfully excites an undamped heavy Higgs boson with twisted angular momentum J=2 and projection Jz=0, which couples to the light Higgs mode (J=1, Jz=0), observable via real-time coupled oscillations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed quantum quench protocol enables undamped heavy Higgs excitation in Balian-Werthamer phases, with the heavy mode coupling to the light Higgs mode, providing a pathway for studying collective modes in topological superfluids.

title: Spin-Orbit Coupling Effects on the Structural and Electronic Properties of Planar Pentagonal p-MS$_{2}$ (M = Si, Ge, and Pb)
summary: Spin-orbit coupling (SOC) plays an important role in determining the structural and electronic properties of recently proposed two-dimensional planar pentagonal materials. In this work, density functional theory calculations are employed to investigate SOC effects in p-MS$_{2}$ systems (M = Si, Ge, and Pb). Our results indicate that the p-SiS$_{2}$ structure is likely unstable, except for p-GeS$_{2}$ and p-PbS$_{2}$. A detailed j-resolved (total angular momentum) orbital analysis reveals that SOC enhances electronic localization, leading to a slight structural contraction and a reconstruction of electronic states near the Fermi level, this effect becoming stronger for heavier M atoms. While p-GeS$_{2}$ remains metallic, SOC drives a metal-semiconductor transition in p-PbS$_{2}$ and opening a quasi-direct band gap of about 0.475 eV. In addition, the conduction band minimum state of p-PbS$_{2}$ exhibits pronounced anisotropy along the S-S bonds. These findings provide insight into SOC-driven structural and electronic reconstruction in planar pentagonal chalcogenides p-MS$_{2}$ and suggest that p-PbS$_{2}$ may be a promising candidate for gas-sensing applications.

AI.tldr: This study uses DFT to investigate spin-orbit coupling (SOC) effects in two-dimensional planar pentagonal p-MS₂ (M = Si, Ge, Pb). p-SiS₂ is likely unstable, while p-GeS₂ and p-PbS₂ are stable. SOC induces structural contraction and electronic reconstruction; p-GeS₂ remains metallic, but SOC drives a metal-semiconductor transition in p-PbS₂, opening a ~0.475 eV quasi-direct band gap. p-PbS₂ is proposed as a promising candidate for gas-sensing applications.
AI.motivation: To understand how spin-orbit coupling affects the structural and electronic properties of two-dimensional planar pentagonal chalcogenides p-MS₂, which are important for next-generation electronic and sensing applications.
AI.method: Density functional theory (DFT) calculations with j-resolved (total angular momentum) orbital analysis to examine SOC effects in p-MS₂ (M = Si, Ge, Pb) systems.
AI.result: p-SiS₂ is likely unstable; p-GeS₂ and p-PbS₂ are stable. SOC enhances electronic localization, causes slight structural contraction, and reconstructs electronic states near the Fermi level. p-GeS₂ remains metallic, while p-PbS₂ undergoes a metal-semiconductor transition with a ~0.475 eV quasi-direct band gap. The conduction band minimum in p-PbS₂ shows pronounced anisotropy along S-S bonds.
AI.conclusion: SOC-driven structural and electronic reconstruction is significant in planar pentagonal chalcogenides, and p-PbS₂ emerges as a promising candidate for gas-sensing applications due to its SOC-induced semiconducting nature and anisotropic electronic properties.

title: Quantum Spin-5/2 Blume-Capel Model in a Random Transverse-Crystalline Field Anisotropy
summary: In this work, we investigate the thermodynamic properties of the quantum Blume-Capel model with spin \( S = 5/2 \) in the presence of transverse and random crystalline fields. The system is described by a Hamiltonian that includes ferromagnetic exchange interactions between nearest neighbors, a longitudinal single-ion anisotropy, and a transverse single-ion anisotropy. Using a mean-field approach based on Bogoliubov's inequality for the Gibbs free energy, we derive the fundamental thermodynamic potential and the equation of state for the magnetization. The influence of the longitudinal and transverse anisotropy parameters on the magnetic ordering and phase transitions is analyzed in detail. We present magnetization versus temperature diagrams for various combinations of the anisotropies, exploring both positive and negative values. Our results reveal that the system exhibits standard second-order phase transitions for most parameter ranges, with no evidence of tricritical behavior. However, for certain positive values of the anisotropies, the model displays a first-order phase transition within the ordered phase, characterized by a jump from a higher-spin ordered state to a lower-spin ordered state. The critical temperatures are shown to be sensitive to the magnitude and sign of the anisotropy parameters. In particular, negative transverse anisotropies favor magnetic order, raising the critical temperature, while positive anisotropies promote disorder, lowering the critical temperature. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of the phase diagram of the \( S = 5/2 \) quantum Blume-Capel model and highlights the role of transverse fields in modifying the critical behavior.

AI.tldr: This paper uses mean-field theory and Bogoliubov's inequality to study the thermodynamic properties and phase transitions of the quantum Blume-Capel model with spin S=5/2 under transverse and random crystalline fields. It finds second-order transitions in most regimes, first-order transitions within the ordered phase for certain positive anisotropies, and that negative transverse anisotropies raise critical temperatures while positive ones lower them.
AI.motivation: To investigate the thermodynamic properties and phase transition behavior of the quantum Blume-Capel model with spin S=5/2, particularly under the combined influence of transverse and random crystalline fields, which has not been comprehensively analyzed before.
AI.method: Mean-field approach based on Bogoliubov's inequality for the Gibbs free energy to derive the thermodynamic potential and equation of state for magnetization.
AI.result: Standard second-order phase transitions for most parameter ranges with no tricritical behavior; first-order phase transitions within the ordered phase (jump from higher-spin to lower-spin ordered state) for certain positive anisotropy values; critical temperatures are sensitive to anisotropy sign and magnitude, with negative transverse anisotropies enhancing magnetic order and positive ones promoting disorder.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a comprehensive phase diagram of the S=5/2 quantum Blume-Capel model, highlighting the significant role of transverse fields in modifying critical behavior and magnetic ordering.

title: Visualizing orbital magnetism in electron doped rhombohedral multilayer graphene
summary: Electron doped rhombohedral multilayer graphene at high displacement field features an exceptionally flat band minimum with near-ideal quantum geometry. Experiments in this regime observe the formation of a 'quarter metal,' in which the electron liquid condenses into a single spin- and valley flavor. Remarkably, recent experiments have found a zero resistance state in the same region of the density- and displacement-field-tuned parameter space, attributed to the formation of a chiral superconductor characterized by a finite-momentum Cooper pair condensate. Here, we use nanoSQUID-on-tip magnetometry to map the orbital magnetization of electron-doped rhombohedral graphene devices ranging in thickness between 3 and 13 layers. Magnetization within the quarter metal phases peaks at finite density, consistent with concentration of the Berry curvature in a finite-momentum 'ring of fire'. Correlating transport and local magnetometry data in a tetralayer sample reveals that the superconducting state has a finite orbital magnetic moment, providing direct evidence of its chiral nature. We further show that widely observed stochastic switching of the resistivity in the metallic regime arises from a density-tuned sign change in the valley-resolved total magnetic moment. This leads to the formation of metastable magnetic domains under typical gate control sequences and can also be harnessed for electric-field controlled switching of orbital moment across the entire device. Unexpectedly, we find magnetic inhomogeneity specific to the apparent normal state of the chiral superconductor, suggestive of a strain-tuned competition between magnetic and non-magnetic ground states. Our results point to a subtle energetic competition underlying the observation of chiral superconductivity in a narrow range of layer numbers.

AI.tldr: Using nanoSQUID-on-tip magnetometry, the authors map orbital magnetization in electron-doped rhombohedral graphene (3-13 layers), providing direct evidence that the superconducting state is chiral (finite orbital magnetic moment), revealing that resistivity switching arises from density-tuned valley magnetic moment sign changes and metastable magnetic domains, and finding magnetic inhomogeneity in the normal state suggestive of strain-tuned competition between magnetic and non-magnetic ground states.
AI.motivation: Recent experiments discovered a zero-resistance state attributed to chiral superconductivity with finite-momentum Cooper pairing in the quarter metal phase of rhombohedral multilayer graphene. Direct evidence of the chiral nature and understanding of the underlying magnetic and orbital properties remain lacking.
AI.method: nanoSQUID-on-tip magnetometry to map orbital magnetization of electron-doped rhombohedral graphene devices (3-13 layers), correlated with transport measurements in tetralayer samples.
AI.result: (1) Magnetization in quarter metal phases peaks at finite density, consistent with Berry curvature concentrated in a finite-momentum 'ring of fire'. (2) The superconducting state has a finite orbital magnetic moment, directly proving its chiral nature. (3) Stochastic resistivity switching arises from density-tuned sign changes in valley-resolved total magnetic moment, forming metastable magnetic domains. (4) Magnetic inhomogeneity is specific to the normal state of the chiral superconductor, suggesting strain-tuned competition between magnetic and non-magnetic ground states.
AI.conclusion: Chiral superconductivity in rhombohedral graphene emerges from a subtle energetic competition between magnetic and non-magnetic ground states, and is observable only in a narrow range of layer numbers.

title: Macroscopic evidence of spatial modulation of conductivity in a microtextured ferromagnetic film
summary: A 75 nm-thick Fe0.5Pt0.5 film is a ferromagnetic metal showing striped magnetic domains in remanence at room temperature. The magnetoresistance is characterized by varying the external temperature and the in-plane magnetic field intensity, thereby affecting its magnetic structure. Qualitatively, the resistivity is well described by using the generalized Ohm's law. High-field magnetotransport properties are successfully explained by considering the competition between the expected metallic behavior and the electron-magnon interaction. In the low-field condition, we size the contribution of the magnetic texture to the macroscopic magnetotransport response by introducing a new quantity. Consistent with the microscopic modulation of the lateral conduction, low-field measurements reveal inhomogeneities attributed to the spatial distribution of ferromagnetic domains and domain walls. By carefully analyzing the macroscopic response near the coercive field, the additional contribution to the resistivity is attributed to the domain walls themselves. In fact, this term could surpass the anisotropic term at low temperatures. In summary, this study demonstrates that spatial magnetic inhomogeneities are not only macroscopically measurable but also comparable in magnitude to other regularly considered terms, mainly at low temperatures.

AI.tldr: The study investigates magnetoresistance in a 75 nm-thick Fe₀.₅Pt₀.₅ film with striped magnetic domains, showing that resistivity follows generalized Ohm's law qualitatively. High-field transport is explained by metallic behavior competing with electron-magnon interactions. Low-field measurements reveal contributions from magnetic texture inhomogeneities, with domain walls adding resistivity that can surpass anisotropic magnetoresistance at low temperatures.
AI.motivation: To understand how spatial magnetic inhomogeneities (ferromagnetic domains and domain walls) contribute to macroscopic magnetoresistance in a ferromagnetic metal with striped domain structure, particularly at low temperatures where domain wall contributions may dominate.
AI.method: Magnetoresistance measurements on a 75 nm-thick Fe₀.₅Pt₀.₅ film with varying temperature and in-plane magnetic field. Qualitative analysis using generalized Ohm's law; high-field analysis considering competition between metallic conduction and electron-magnon scattering; low-field analysis introducing a new quantity to quantify magnetic texture contributions to transport.
AI.result: High-field transport governed by metallic behavior and electron-magnon interaction competition. Low-field measurements reveal resistive inhomogeneities from ferromagnetic domain/domain wall spatial distribution. Domain walls contribute additional resistivity near the coercive field, which can surpass the anisotropic magnetoresistance term at low temperatures.
AI.conclusion: Spatial magnetic inhomogeneities produce macroscopically measurable contributions to resistivity comparable in magnitude to conventional transport terms, especially at low temperatures where domain wall resistivity can dominate over anisotropic magnetoresistance.

title: Breaking Bipartite and Time Reversal Symmetries by Fusing Porphine Unit in-between two Zigzag-edge Graphene Nanoribbons
summary: Hybrid structure of two zigzag-edge graphene nanoribbons with a fused porphine ring in between, results in two distinct nearly degenerate ground states: a semiconducting antiferromagnetic state and a conducting ferromagnetic state with unequal and opposite Fermi velocities of majority and minority spins, the former having slightly higher stability. Such ground states result from the broken bipartite symmetry induced by the porphine ring. The incorporation of different transition metal atoms in the porphine cavity reduces their energy difference but keeps their electronic properties mostly unchanged. The splitting of the $d$-orbitals in the distorted square-planar ligand field of porphine produces a high spin ground state that breaks the global time reversal symmetry ($\mathcal{T}$). The opposite Fermi velocities of the majority and minority spins in the ferromagnetic ground state and lower sensitivity of the conducting majority spin channel to the edge disorder, make this class of quasi-one-dimensional hybrid structures promising for dual spin-filtering device applications.

AI.tldr: Hybrid zigzag-edge graphene nanoribbons with a porphine ring exhibit two nearly degenerate ground states: a semiconducting antiferromagnetic state and a conducting ferromagnetic state with opposite Fermi velocities for different spins, the latter promising for dual spin-filtering devices.
AI.motivation: To explore the electronic and magnetic properties of hybrid graphene-porphine nanostructures and their potential for spintronic applications.
AI.method: Density functional theory calculations on hybrid structures of zigzag-edge graphene nanoribbons fused with a porphine ring, with and without transition metal atom incorporation.
AI.result: Two nearly degenerate ground states found: semiconducting antiferromagnetic and conducting ferromagnetic with opposite Fermi velocities for majority/minority spins. Transition metal incorporation reduces energy difference between states but preserves electronic properties. d-orbital splitting in porphine produces high-spin ground state breaking time-reversal symmetry.
AI.conclusion: The opposite Fermi velocities and lower sensitivity of the conducting majority spin channel to edge disorder make these structures promising for dual spin-filtering device applications.

title: Electron momentum densities from QSGW and $G^0W^0$: Revealing the role of many-body effects within the reduced density matrix
summary: The ground-state many-body electron momentum density, which can be probed by x-ray Compton scattering, holds insights into the electronic structure of materials. Comparisons between the measured so-called Compton profiles and the theoretical ones are invaluable in assessing the successes and failures of the methodology used to generate the theoretical ground-state electronic structure. Here, we present calculations of the Compton profiles of Li, Si, Cr, and Ni using the state-of-the-art QSGW method within the Questaal package compared with density functional theory (DFT), one-shot $GW$ ($G^0W^0$) predictions and with experiment. This comparison reveals significant differences between the QSGW and $G^0W^0$ methods which we attribute to the distinction between the single particle density provided by the QSGW method and the many-body density that we construct from the $G^0W^0$ theory; although in general the QSGW description of the electronic structure is superior to that of $G^0W^0$, we find the use of the many-body reduced density matrix is key to improving the agreement of the Compton profile with experiment.

AI.tldr: This paper computes Compton profiles for Li, Si, Cr, and Ni using QSGW, DFT, and G0W0 methods, comparing them with experiments. It finds that QSGW provides superior electronic structure description, but using the many-body reduced density matrix from G0W0 is key to better agreement with experimental Compton profiles.
AI.motivation: To assess the successes and failures of different theoretical methods (QSGW, DFT, G0W0) in describing ground-state electronic structure by comparing computed Compton profiles with experimental measurements.
AI.method: Compton profiles are calculated using the QSGW method within the Questaal package, DFT, and one-shot G0W0 (G0W0), and compared with experimental data for Li, Si, Cr, and Ni.
AI.result: Significant differences between QSGW and G0W0 results are found, attributed to the distinction between the single-particle density (QSGW) and the many-body density constructed from G0W0 theory. QSGW generally offers superior electronic structure, but the many-body reduced density matrix from G0W0 improves agreement with experiment.
AI.conclusion: While QSGW provides a better overall electronic structure description, incorporating the many-body reduced density matrix is essential for achieving closer agreement with experimental Compton profiles.

title: Thermodynamic and magnetocaloric properties of a triangular spin-1/2 cluster with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction
summary: We present a theoretical investigation of the magnetic and thermodynamic properties of the triangular spin-1/2 cluster with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction, described by a spin-1/2 Heisenberg Hamiltonian with antisymmetric exchange interactions. The energy spectrum and ground-state phase diagram reveal the presence of ferromagnetic (FM), ferrimagnetic (FI), and frustrated (FR) phases, strongly influenced by the total spin and the DM interaction. We analyze magnetization and susceptibility, showing that at low temperatures the system exhibits a characteristic 1/3 magnetization plateau, while thermal fluctuations suppress magnetic order at higher temperatures. The entropy and specific heat display residual entropies due to ground-state degeneracies, Schottky-type anomalies at intermediate temperatures, and additional low-temperature features related to phase transitions. Particular attention is given to the magnetocaloric effect (MCE), characterized by both direct and inverse regimes depending on the magnetic field variation. We find that the DM interaction enhances the complexity of the MCE, leading to nontrivial entropy variations as a function of the magnetic field. These results provide insights into the role of frustration and anisotropy in tuning the MCE of properties triangular spin clusters, with relevance to \mathrm{Cu}_{3}-based molecular magnets.

AI.tldr: The paper theoretically investigates a triangular spin-1/2 cluster with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, revealing FM, FI, and FR phases, a 1/3 magnetization plateau, Schottky anomalies, and complex magnetocaloric effects with direct/inverse regimes enhanced by DM interaction.
AI.motivation: To understand how frustration and antisymmetric exchange (DM interaction) influence the magnetic, thermodynamic, and magnetocaloric properties of triangular spin-1/2 clusters, with relevance to Cu₃-based molecular magnets.
AI.method: Theoretical investigation using a spin-1/2 Heisenberg Hamiltonian with antisymmetric DM exchange interactions; analysis of energy spectrum, ground-state phase diagrams, magnetization, susceptibility, entropy, specific heat, and magnetocaloric effect.
AI.result: Identification of FM, FI, and FR phases; observation of a 1/3 magnetization plateau at low temperatures; residual entropies from ground-state degeneracies; Schottky-type anomalies; direct and inverse MCE regimes; DM interaction enriches MCE complexity with nontrivial entropy variations.
AI.conclusion: Frustration and DM interaction are key tunable parameters for controlling the magnetocaloric effect in triangular spin clusters, providing insights for Cu₃-based molecular magnet applications.

title: Accelerated Discovery of Nitrogen-Coordinated Dual-Atom Hydrogen Evolution Reaction Electrocatalysts via Machine Learning Potentials
summary: The hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is central to sustainable hydrogen production, and nitrogen coordinated dual atom catalysts (DACs) offer a promising route to noble metal activity at low cost. Yet their vast compositional and coordination design space remains underexplored, as density functional theory (DFT) screening at scale is prohibitive. Here, we map the HER landscape of graphene supported TM2@Nx-Gr DACs, screening 23 transition metals across 20 nitrogen coordination motifs using a machine learning potential (MLP) benchmarked against DFT. Intermediate coordination (2N to 4N) consistently yields near-optimal ΔGH*, with Ti2@2Na, Mn2@2Na, Fe2@2Na, Cu2@2Na, Rh2@2Na, Zr2@2Na, Zr2@2Nb, Zr2@2Nc, Nb2@2Nc, Zr2@2Nd, Mn2@2Ne, Mn2@2Nf, Ti2@3Na, Au2@3Na, Fe2@3Na, Pd2@3Nb, Rh2@3Nc, Rh2@3Nd, Au2@3Nd, V2@4Na, Ti2@4Nb, Pd2@4Nb, Ti2@4Nc, Cr2@4Nd, Ni2@4Nd, Cu2@4Nd emerging as standout, synthesizable candidates, most exhibiting metallic or narrow gap (<0.25 eV) character. The MLP reaches near-DFT accuracy, with a mean absolute error of 80 meV for Gibbs binding free energies at orders of magnitude lower computational cost, establishing MLP driven screening as a practical engine for next-generation catalyst discovery.

AI.tldr: Machine learning potential-driven screening of 23 transition metals across 20 nitrogen coordination motifs identifies 27 standout dual atom catalysts for hydrogen evolution reaction, achieving near-DFT accuracy (80 meV MAE) at dramatically lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: To efficiently explore the vast compositional and coordination design space of nitrogen-coordinated dual atom catalysts (DACs) for hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), which is impractical via conventional DFT screening.
AI.method: Developed a machine learning potential (MLP) benchmarked against DFT to screen TM2@Nx-Gr DACs, covering 23 transition metals and 20 nitrogen coordination motifs, and computed Gibbs binding free energies (ΔGH*) to evaluate HER activity.
AI.result: Identified 27 promising DAC candidates with near-optimal ΔGH*, mostly metallic or narrow-gap (<0.25 eV) semiconductors; MLP achieved 80 meV MAE against DFT with orders of magnitude lower computational cost.
AI.conclusion: MLP-driven screening is a practical and efficient engine for discovering next-generation HER catalysts, effectively exploring the DAC design space that DFT alone cannot cover at scale.

title: Electronic correlations driving Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity
summary: We explicitly account for electron-electron interactions when modeling low-dimensional helical organic molecules. We show that competition between various hopping channels, together with interaction-induced double- and superexchange mechanisms, can stabilize non-collinear helical magnetic order. The resulting single-electron bands exhibit partial spin polarization, a manifestation of $p$-wave magnetism. Using density-matrix renormalization group, cluster perturbation theory, and Monte Carlo methods, we find that even vanishingly small spin-orbit coupling triggers strong spin selectivity at temperatures significantly above the spin-orbit scale. While strong correlations are essential for this mechanism, long-range spin ordering is not required. We thus propose non-collinear spin correlations driven by Coulomb interactions as an explanation of chirality-induced spin selectivity and discuss connections to experiments.

AI.tldr: Electron-electron interactions in low-dimensional helical organic molecules can stabilize non-collinear helical magnetic order via competition between hopping channels and double-/superexchange mechanisms, leading to p-wave magnetism and strong spin selectivity at temperatures above the spin-orbit scale, even without long-range order. This offers a Coulomb-interaction-driven explanation for chirality-induced spin selectivity.
AI.motivation: To explain chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS) in helical organic molecules by accounting for electron-electron interactions, which have been largely overlooked in previous theoretical treatments that focused primarily on spin-orbit coupling effects.
AI.method: Theoretical modeling of low-dimensional helical organic molecules with explicit electron-electron interactions, analyzed using density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG), cluster perturbation theory, and Monte Carlo methods.
AI.result: Competition between hopping channels and interaction-driven double-/superexchange mechanisms stabilize non-collinear helical magnetic order. Even vanishingly small spin-orbit coupling triggers strong spin selectivity at temperatures significantly above the spin-orbit scale, without requiring long-range spin ordering.
AI.conclusion: Non-collinear spin correlations driven by Coulomb interactions, rather than spin-orbit coupling alone, provide a robust explanation for chirality-induced spin selectivity, with strong correlations essential but long-range order unnecessary.

title: Surface Originated Cross-Field Anomalous Transport in Magnetoelectric Multilayers
summary: In material systems with slab geometry, the surface contribution to physical responses is commonly expected to diminish rapidly with increasing thickness, giving way to the bulk response. Here, we show that this conventional wisdom is violated in a class of gate-induced responses, including gate-induced orbital and spin magnetization as well as cross-field anomalous thermoelectric transport. We develop a general framework for these effects, which naturally decomposes the total response into surface- and bulk-contributions treated on equal footing. Remarkably, the volume-averaged surface contribution remains finite in the thick-slab limit and exhibits the same thickness scaling as the bulk term. Furthermore, the surface response originates from band geometric quantities distinct from those in the bulk, being constrained solely by surface symmetries. As a result, it can dominate the overall response when the bulk contribution is symmetry-forbidden. Taking MnBi$_2$Te$_4$ multilayers as an example, we predict a strong surface-dominated cross-field anomalous Nernst effect arising from surface Berry curvature, which is readily accessible to experimental detection. These findings reveal a previously overlooked significance of surface response and open a new direction in the study of surface quantum geometry.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that in slab materials, surface contributions to gate-induced responses (like orbital/spin magnetization and anomalous thermoelectric transport) do not vanish with increasing thickness but instead scale similarly to bulk contributions. The surface response arises from distinct band geometric quantities governed by surface symmetries and can dominate when bulk contributions are symmetry-forbidden, as demonstrated with a surface-dominated anomalous Nernst effect in MnBi₂Te₄ multilayers.
AI.motivation: To challenge the conventional expectation that surface contributions in slab geometries diminish with thickness, and to demonstrate that gate-induced responses can exhibit finite surface contributions that scale similarly to bulk responses, thus revealing previously overlooked surface quantum geometric effects.
AI.method: Development of a general theoretical framework that decomposes gate-induced responses into surface and bulk contributions on equal footing, analyzing their thickness scaling and symmetry constraints. The framework is applied to MnBi₂Te₄ multilayers as a case study.
AI.result: Volume-averaged surface contribution remains finite in the thick-slab limit with the same thickness scaling as the bulk term; surface response originates from distinct band geometric quantities constrained by surface symmetries; a strong surface-dominated cross-field anomalous Nernst effect is predicted in MnBi₂Te₄.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal a previously overlooked significance of surface response in slab geometries and open a new direction in studying surface quantum geometry, particularly relevant for gate-induced responses.

title: Optical Cooling of Nuclear Spins in a CdTe/CdZnTe Quantum Well: The Impact of Kinetic Local Fields on Cooling Efficiency
summary: The efficiency of optical cooling of nuclear spins in a CdTe/CdZnTe quantum well is investigated as a function of an external magnetic field. Our results confirm that there is indeed an optimal external magnetic field for optical cooling. We associate it with the kinetic local field $B_{KL}$ defined by the heating rate of the spin-spin reservoir due to the fluctuations of the hyperfine interaction. We also propose an experimental technique for measuring $B_{KL}$. For our sample we find that $B_{KL}=1.0\pm0.4$ G and it is independent of the electron polarization and pump power. The measured values of the kinetic local fields are in good agreement with a theoretical calculation $B_{KL} = 0.7$ G, taking into account indirect spin-spin interactions of Cd and Te nuclear spins and their considerably different hyperfine constants. The hyperfine constants of the magnetic isotopes of Cd and Te in CdTe are estimated.

AI.tldr: Optical cooling of nuclear spins in a CdTe/CdZnTe quantum well has an optimal external magnetic field, linked to the kinetic local field B_KL (~1.0 G), which matches theoretical predictions (~0.7 G) considering indirect spin-spin interactions and hyperfine constants of Cd and Te isotopes.
AI.motivation: To investigate the efficiency of optical cooling of nuclear spins as a function of external magnetic field and identify the optimal field, as well as to measure the kinetic local field B_KL.
AI.method: Experimental optical cooling of nuclear spins in a CdTe/CdZnTe quantum well under varying external magnetic fields, with theoretical modeling of B_KL using indirect spin-spin interactions and hyperfine constants of Cd and Te magnetic isotopes.
AI.result: An optimal external magnetic field exists for optical cooling, defined by B_KL = 1.0 ± 0.4 G, independent of electron polarization and pump power. Theoretical calculation yields B_KL = 0.7 G. Hyperfine constants of Cd and Te magnetic isotopes in CdTe are estimated.
AI.conclusion: The kinetic local field B_KL governs the optimal external magnetic field for optical cooling. The proposed experimental technique for measuring B_KL is validated by the agreement between measured and calculated values.

title: Spectroscopic evidence for a molecular orbital Kondo insulator
summary: A Kondo insulator (KI) is a prototypical example of a highly entangled phase of matter, where many-body interactions between local moments and delocalized electrons engender the non-magnetic insulating ground state. Conventionally, the local moments arise from atomic multiplet states with a narrow bandwidth, limiting Kondo coherence to low temperatures. Here, we realize a new paradigm for constructing the KI state with hybridized molecular orbitals in FeSb2. Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) at the Fe L-edge reveals distinct signatures of band-like continuum states and localized states. Comparisons with first-principles calculations establish a mixed-configuration ground state with hybridized Fe d-Sb p molecular orbitals as basis states. By systematically investigating the RIXS momentum, temperature, and doping dependences, we find propagating collective modes commensurate with many-body charge and spin excitations. Our results pave the way for understanding the emerging class of unconventional d electron insulators and engineering high temperature Kondo many-body states.

AI.tldr: This paper reports a new paradigm for Kondo insulators (KI) using hybridized molecular orbitals in FeSb₂, observed via RIXS at Fe L-edge. The study reveals mixed-configuration ground states, band-like continua, localized states, and propagating collective modes (charge/spin excitations), enabling higher-temperature Kondo many-body states.
AI.motivation: Conventional Kondo insulators rely on atomic multiplet states with narrow bandwidth, limiting Kondo coherence to low temperatures. The authors aim to construct a KI state using hybridized molecular orbitals to overcome this temperature limitation and explore unconventional d-electron insulators.
AI.method: Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) at the Fe L-edge, combined with first-principles calculations, to probe electronic structure, momentum/temperature/doping dependence, and collective modes in FeSb₂.
AI.result: Observation of band-like continuum states and localized states, a mixed-configuration ground state with hybridized Fe d-Sb p molecular orbitals, and propagating collective modes commensurate with many-body charge and spin excitations.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a new paradigm for KI states via molecular orbital hybridization, paving the way for understanding unconventional d-electron insulators and engineering high-temperature Kondo many-body states.

title: Engineering Quantum Criticality in the Integer Quantum Hall Regime through a Screening Layer
summary: Disorder-induced localization of electrons and electron-electron interaction are among the most fundamental problems in condensed matter physics. In two-dimensional electron systems, extensive studies have led to the emergence of a scaling picture, characterized by a set of universal critical exponents that govern the transitions between the integer quantum Hall plateaus. From the temperature dependence of the plateau-to-plateau transitions, experiments primarily report k ~ 0.42, implying a dynamic exponent z = 1, consistent with a theoretical picture where electrons have a long-range (1/r) interaction. Theory also predicts that z = 2 for short-range electron interaction, but an experimental verification has remained elusive. Here, we directly probe the influence of Coulomb interaction on these transitions using a bilayer electron system confined to a GaAs double quantum well device. The two layers are in close proximity, with an interlayer distance approximately equal to the magnetic length at the relevant magnetic fields. By tuning the electron density in the top layer, we access both insulating and metallic phases of the electrons in this layer as a function of magnetic field, allowing in-situ control of the unscreened and screened interaction strengths in the bottom layer as it goes through its plateau-to-plateau transitions. In the unscreened case, we measure k ~ 0.42 consistent with the widely reported value. More importantly, when screening is introduced, k is reduced to ~ 0.22, implying z = 2. Our results provide direct experimental evidence for the role of electron-electron interaction in determining critical behavior in the quantum Hall regime, and demonstrate screening as a powerful tuning parameter for engineering quantum criticality.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the effect of electron-electron interaction on quantum Hall plateau-to-plateau transitions using a bilayer GaAs double quantum well. By tuning screening via a top layer, the dynamic exponent changes from z=1 (unscreened, long-range Coulomb, k~0.42) to z=2 (screened, short-range interaction, k~0.22), directly confirming theoretical predictions.
AI.motivation: To provide direct experimental evidence of how electron-electron interaction (long-range vs. short-range) governs the critical behavior in quantum Hall plateau-to-plateau transitions, particularly verifying the theoretical prediction that z=2 for short-range interactions, which had remained elusive.
AI.method: A bilayer electron system in a GaAs double quantum well with closely spaced layers (interlayer distance ~ magnetic length). The top layer electron density is tuned to control insulating/metallic phases, providing in-situ control of unscreened vs. screened Coulomb interaction in the bottom layer during its plateau-to-plateau transitions. Critical exponent k is extracted from temperature dependence.
AI.result: Unscreened case yields k ~ 0.42 (z=1, long-range interaction). Screened case reduces k to ~ 0.22 (z=2, short-range interaction).
AI.conclusion: Direct experimental evidence that electron-electron interaction determines critical behavior in quantum Hall transitions, with screening serving as a tuning parameter for quantum criticality. Confirms theoretical predictions for both long-range (z=1) and short-range (z=2) interaction regimes.

title: Topological spin-texture transitions in van der Waals magnets revealed by X-ray Fourier transform holography
summary: Nontrivial topological spin-textures, such as skyrmions, merons, bimerons, and skyrmioniums, are envisioned as robust building blocks for future memory and logic devices. Controllable transformations between these states require a quantum-mechanical description of electronic degrees of freedom and atomic-scale insight beyond existing phenomenological models. Here, we report an atomic-scale investigation of topological phase transitions and their protection in the two-dimensional van der Waals ferromagnet Fe$_3$GeTe$_2$ (FGT) using a combined experimental-theoretical approach. Synchrotron-based Fourier transform holography directly images labyrinth domains, isolated skyrmions, mixed labyrinth-skyrmion phases, and skyrmion bags with high spatial resolution. We compare these observations to simulations based on an electronic lattice Hamiltonian that captures both metallicity and relativistic spin-orbit coupling in FGT. By systematically exploring a broad range of temperatures and magnetic fields, we map the mechanisms governing topological transitions and their stability. This sequential-integrated experimental-theoretical framework advances understanding of spin-texture interactions and enables precise control of external tuning parameters. Our results establish a platform for creating, stabilizing, and manipulating topological states, paving the way for engineered spin-texture transitions in next-generation spintronic technologies.

AI.tldr: This paper combines synchrotron-based Fourier transform holography with electronic lattice Hamiltonian simulations to image and explain topological spin-texture transitions (skyrmions, labyrinths, skyrmion bags) in the 2D van der Waals ferromagnet Fe₃GeTe₂, establishing a platform for controlled manipulation of topological states for spintronic applications.
AI.motivation: Existing phenomenological models cannot provide the quantum-mechanical atomic-scale description needed to understand and control transformations between topological spin-textures (skyrmions, merons, bimerons, skyrmioniums), which are promising for memory and logic devices.
AI.method: Combined experimental-theoretical approach: (1) synchrotron-based Fourier transform holography for direct high-resolution imaging of spin textures in Fe₃GeTe₂, and (2) simulations based on an electronic lattice Hamiltonian incorporating metallicity and relativistic spin-orbit coupling. Systematic exploration across temperatures and magnetic fields.
AI.result: Direct imaging of labyrinth domains, isolated skyrmions, mixed labyrinth-skyrmion phases, and skyrmion bags. Mapping of mechanisms governing topological transitions and their stability. Agreement between experimental observations and Hamiltonian-based simulations.
AI.conclusion: The sequential-integrated experimental-theoretical framework advances understanding of spin-texture interactions, enables precise control of external tuning parameters, and establishes a platform for creating, stabilizing, and manipulating topological states for next-generation spintronic technologies.

title: Carrier-coupled ultrafast structural dynamics and interlayer energy transport of supported transition metal dichalcogenide heterostructures
summary: Understanding the electronic coupling and energy flow across layered two-dimensional heterostructures (HSs) is crucial to the exploitation of carrier and phonon transports as well as thermal management in next-generation optoelectronic devices. By using reflection ultrafast electron diffraction, we directly examine photoinduced out-of-plane structural dynamics of supported MoS2/WS2 bilayer HSs and their individual monolayers. Experimental evidence reveals the launch of ultrafast carrier-coupled intralayer atomic motions due to interlayer charge transfer across the van der Waals (vdW) heterojunctions that is absent for individual monolayers. Such a notable carrier-lattice correlation is in addition to the electronic coupling manifested in the enhanced optical absorption for HSs. Also, different pathways of energy flow as a result of carrier-phonon coupling and phonon scattering are reported with the corresponding characteristic times. On longer timescales, relaxation of thermalized atomic motions can be sufficiently described by a thermal transport model. A higher thermal boundary conductance (TBC) across MoS2/WS2 HSs is obtained compared to those at the monolayer-substrate interfaces; however, the similar TBC values suggest comparable couplings of phonons across vdW contacts. These results further shed light on the optical, phonon, and interfacial thermal properties of vertically-stacked vdW HSs.

AI.tldr: This study uses reflection ultrafast electron diffraction to directly observe photoinduced out-of-plane structural dynamics in MoS2/WS2 bilayer heterostructures, revealing ultrafast carrier-coupled intralayer atomic motions driven by interlayer charge transfer, distinct energy flow pathways, and comparable thermal boundary conductances across van der Waals contacts.
AI.motivation: Understanding electronic coupling and energy flow across layered 2D heterostructures is essential for carrier/phonon transport and thermal management in next-generation optoelectronic devices.
AI.method: Reflection ultrafast electron diffraction was used to directly examine photoinduced out-of-plane structural dynamics of supported MoS2/WS2 bilayer heterostructures and their individual monolayers.
AI.result: Ultrafast carrier-coupled intralayer atomic motions were observed due to interlayer charge transfer across vdW heterojunctions, absent in monolayers. Different energy flow pathways with characteristic times were identified. Higher thermal boundary conductance across MoS2/WS2 HSs was found compared to monolayer-substrate interfaces, but TBC values were similar across vdW contacts.
AI.conclusion: The results illuminate optical, phonon, and interfacial thermal properties of vertically-stacked van der Waals heterostructures, with comparable phonon coupling across vdW contacts.

title: Carrier Localization in Pnictogen-Based Chalcohalides from Defect-Bound Hot Polarons
summary: Pnictogen-based solar absorbers have gained prominence as promising nontoxic and stable alternatives to lead-halide perovskites (LHPs), but are severely limited by carrier localization, preventing their performance from approaching those of LHPs. Recent efforts have uncovered routes to overcome carrier localization, but these early efforts only considered intrinsic factors. Herein, we push beyond these limited early efforts, examining the role of defects, not only on cold carriers but also hot carriers. Focusing on the structurally one-dimensional pnictogen chalcohalide BiSBr, we find that whilst this material intrinsically does not exhibit carrier localization, vacancies introduced during synthesis or post-treatment lead to pronounced extrinsic self-trapping via the formation of defect-bound hot polarons-excited charge-carriers strongly coupled to local defect-induced vibrational modes. These above-gap defect states divert hot carriers from cooling to the band edge, thus depleting the mobile carrier population. Our findings establish the key role of defect-bound hot polarons in mediating extrinsic localization and offer new mechanistic insights into the interplay between defects, lattice coupling, and excited-state charge-carrier transport, which are critical to designing efficient perovskite-inspired solar absorbers.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that defects, not intrinsic properties, cause carrier localization in the pnictogen chalcohalide BiSBr via defect-bound hot polarons, explaining why these materials underperform compared to lead-halide perovskites.
AI.motivation: Pnictogen-based solar absorbers are promising nontoxic alternatives to lead-halide perovskites but suffer from carrier localization that limits their performance. Prior work only considered intrinsic factors; this work extends to the role of defects.
AI.method: The authors studied BiSBr as a model system, examining how vacancies introduced during synthesis or post-treatment affect carrier dynamics, specifically focusing on defect-bound hot polarons and their impact on hot carrier cooling.
AI.result: BiSBr intrinsically lacks carrier localization, but vacancies cause extrinsic self-trapping via defect-bound hot polarons. These above-gap defect states divert hot carriers from cooling to the band edge, depleting the mobile carrier population.
AI.conclusion: Defect-bound hot polarons mediate extrinsic localization in pnictogen-based absorbers. The interplay between defects, lattice coupling, and excited-state charge-carrier transport is critical for designing efficient perovskite-inspired solar absorbers.

title: Coherent and Dissipative Spin Torques in Quantum Dots: A Unified Framework for Quantum Spin Dynamics
summary: The manipulation of single spins through spin-polarized tunneling opens new routes for quantum control at the atomic scale. We present a theoretical framework describing spin-transfer, spin torques and spin resonance in molecular quantum dots weakly coupled to magnetic electrodes. By deriving a Lindblad master equation from microscopic tunneling processes, we capture both coherent exchange interactions and dissipative spin torque effects within a unified approach. We analyze how charge transport through localized orbitals influences spin dynamics and show that modulating the tunneling rates in time can induce electron spin resonance. This framework is further extended to coupled spin systems, revealing how spin coherence and entanglement respond to local spin torques and highlighting sources of transport-driven decoherence. Our results provide a general model to interpret spin-resolved tunneling experiments and extend classical spin torque concepts into the quantum regime.

AI.tldr: A theoretical framework using a Lindblad master equation describes spin-transfer, spin torques, and spin resonance in molecular quantum dots weakly coupled to magnetic electrodes, unifying coherent exchange interactions and dissipative spin torque effects.
AI.motivation: To provide a unified theoretical description of single-spin manipulation via spin-polarized tunneling, capturing both coherent and dissipative spin dynamics in molecular quantum dots, and to extend classical spin torque concepts into the quantum regime.
AI.method: Derivation of a Lindblad master equation from microscopic tunneling processes to model spin-transfer, spin torques, and electron spin resonance in molecular quantum dots weakly coupled to magnetic electrodes.
AI.result: The framework captures coherent exchange interactions and dissipative spin torque effects; shows that time-modulated tunneling rates can induce electron spin resonance; reveals how spin coherence and entanglement respond to local spin torques in coupled spin systems; identifies sources of transport-driven decoherence.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a general model for interpreting spin-resolved tunneling experiments and extends classical spin torque concepts into the quantum regime.

title: Charting the thermodynamic stability of hybrid perovskite alloys with machine learning
summary: Alloy-based perovskite solar cells offer tunable properties and improved stability, but their complexity has impeded accurate modeling, hindering development. We present a machine-learning (ML) accelerated atomistic modeling approach for the phase stability of (Cs/FA)Pb(Br/I)3 and (Cs/FA)Sn(Br/I)3 perovskites, with FA being formamidinium. To make such quaternary alloys tractable, we adopt a two-level ML strategy, combining 1) graph neural network interatomic potentials trained on density functional theory data for efficient structure relaxations with 2) secondary ML models for direct energy prediction from unrelaxed structures. These models enable computations of free energy landscapes across compositions and phases, capturing alloy disorder and FA molecular orientations. Our results reveal narrower stable composition regions for the Sn-based system compared to its Pb-based counterpart, limiting options for compositional engineering. Maximum stability occurs at high I content, and no stabilization is observed near the center of the composition space. Our results guide the design of stable perovskites.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a two-level machine learning approach combining GNN interatomic potentials and direct energy prediction models to study phase stability of quaternary (Cs/FA)(Pb/Sn)(Br/I)3 perovskite alloys, finding narrower stability regions for Sn-based systems and maximum stability at high I content.
AI.motivation: Alloy-based perovskite solar cells offer tunable properties and improved stability, but their complexity has impeded accurate modeling, hindering development.
AI.method: Two-level ML strategy: 1) graph neural network interatomic potentials trained on DFT data for efficient structure relaxations, 2) secondary ML models for direct energy prediction from unrelaxed structures, enabling free energy landscape computations across compositions and phases.
AI.result: Narrower stable composition regions for Sn-based system compared to Pb-based counterpart; maximum stability at high I content; no stabilization near the center of composition space.
AI.conclusion: Results guide the design of stable perovskites by revealing limited compositional engineering options for Sn-based systems.

title: Magnetic precession induced spin accumulation in collinear antiferromagnets
summary: Generating and characterizing uniform and staggered spin polarization in antiferromagnets is one of the key challenges for antiferromagnetic spintronic technology. Here, we perform perturbative theory, group-theoretical symmetry analysis, low energy and ab initio simulations to propose that the magnetic precession near the equilibrium magnetic axis could generate finite uniform and staggered spin polarization at the opposite magnetic sublattices (referring to total magnetic and Néel vector generation) in a single AFM semiconductors. This response does not require the heterojunction setup and could eliminate the lattice mismatch issues at the junction. Through scrutinizing all symmetrically-protected vanishing magnetic moment groups and especially focusing on parity-time (PT ) invariant groups, we identify the symmetry constraints that describe the staggered spin accumulation responses, and disclose their fieldlike and dampinglike characters. This unravels a hidden spin accumulation mode in AFM semiconductors. Furthermore, we simulate such an effect using a perturbative approach and suggest that electric gate field and Floquet light-dressing can effectively manipulate these responses.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that magnetic precession near equilibrium can generate uniform and staggered spin polarization in single AFM semiconductors without heterojunctions, identified via symmetry analysis and simulated with perturbative and ab initio methods, with manipulation possible via electric gates and Floquet light.
AI.motivation: A key challenge in antiferromagnetic spintronics is generating and controlling uniform and staggered spin polarization in antiferromagnets. Existing approaches often require heterojunctions which suffer from lattice mismatch issues.
AI.method: Perturbative theory, group-theoretical symmetry analysis, low-energy effective modeling, and ab initio simulations. Symmetry constraints are derived from parity-time (PT) invariant groups and vanishing magnetic moment groups.
AI.result: Magnetic precession near equilibrium can generate both uniform (total magnetic) and staggered (Néel vector) spin polarization in single AFM semiconductors. The response exhibits fieldlike and dampinglike characters. The effect can be manipulated via electric gate fields and Floquet light-dressing.
AI.conclusion: This work reveals a hidden spin accumulation mode in AFM semiconductors, enabling generation of staggered spin polarization without heterojunctions, thus eliminating lattice mismatch issues.

title: Hysteretic Acoustic Band Structures in Shape-Memory Composite Thin Rods
summary: We investigate the propagation of longitudinal elastic waves in one-dimensional periodic composite rods composed of alternating segments of a shape-memory alloy (NiTiCu) and a polymer spacer (Parylene C). In the thin-rod regime, the longitudinal phase velocity reduces to $c=\sqrt{E/ρ}$, which coincides with the regime in which the elastic modulus of NiTiCu has been measured directly through its acoustic response across the martensitic transformation. Using the standard transfer-matrix method along the heating and cooling branches of the transformation separately, we compute the Bloch band structure of the infinite periodic system and the transmission spectrum of finite composite rods. Because the elastic modulus of NiTiCu follows different paths upon heating and cooling, the same external temperature within the transformation interval corresponds to two different phase fractions and, consequently, to two different phononic spectra. The resulting hysteresis of the underlying material is thus transferred to the collective acoustic response of the periodic structure: stop-band edges trace closed loops in the temperature--frequency plane, and the transmission coefficient of a finite rod at a fixed temperature depends on the previous thermal history. We further show that the geometric filling fraction of the active segment provides a complementary tuning mechanism, modifying the width of the spectral hysteresis loops and the position of specific gap closures independently of temperature. These results illustrate how a first-order structural phase transition with intrinsic thermal hysteresis manifests itself in the dispersion relation of a periodic elastic medium.

AI.tldr: This paper studies longitudinal elastic waves in 1D periodic composite rods made of shape-memory alloy (NiTiCu) and polymer (Parylene C). Using the transfer-matrix method, they show that the martensitic transformation hysteresis in NiTiCu transfers to the phononic band structure, causing temperature-history-dependent stop-band edges and transmission spectra.
AI.motivation: To understand how the intrinsic thermal hysteresis of a first-order structural phase transition (martensitic transformation) in a shape-memory alloy manifests in the collective acoustic response of a periodic composite structure.
AI.method: The study employs the standard transfer-matrix method to compute Bloch band structures (infinite system) and transmission spectra (finite rods) for 1D periodic composites of NiTiCu and Parylene C, analyzing heating and cooling branches separately due to the different elastic modulus paths of NiTiCu across the martensitic transformation.
AI.result: The hysteresis of NiTiCu's elastic modulus transfers to the phononic spectrum: stop-band edges form closed hysteresis loops in the temperature-frequency plane, and transmission at a fixed temperature depends on thermal history. The geometric filling fraction of the active segment provides an additional tuning mechanism independent of temperature, modifying hysteresis loop width and gap closure positions.
AI.conclusion: A first-order structural phase transition with intrinsic thermal hysteresis directly manifests in the dispersion relation of a periodic elastic medium, offering dual control via temperature history and geometric filling fraction for tunable phononic properties.
